Ibn al-Qayyim, Commentary on Surah 53, verses 1–2:

Allah the Exalted said, concerning His Prophet, mentioning what He bestowed upon him of purity and freedom from what might afflict others: ﴿By the star when it sets, your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾.

So, "has not strayed" (mā ḍalla) is evidence of the perfection of his knowledge and understanding, and that he is upon the manifest truth; and "nor has he erred" (wa mā ghawā) is evidence of the perfection of his guidance and that he is the most righteous of the worlds. Thus he is perfect in his knowledge and in his action. He described his successors after him with this same quality and commanded that they be followed in their way, saying:

"Upon you is my sunnah and the sunnah of the rightly-guided, rightly-directed caliphs after me."

Related by al-Tirmidhi and others.

Thus al-rāshid is the opposite of al-ghāwī, and al-mahdī is the opposite of al-ḍāll.

(Section)

Among this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿By the star when it sets. Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred, nor does he speak from desire﴾.

He, glorified be He, swore by the star at its setting to declare His Messenger free and innocent of what his enemies attributed to him of error and deviation.

People have differed about what is meant by "the star" (al-najm). Al-Kalbi said, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: He swore by the Qur'an when it was revealed to His Messenger in installments (najman), four verses, three verses, and a surah, and between its beginning and its end was twenty years. ʿAtaʾ related the same from him, and this is the view of Muqatil, al-Dahhak, and Mujahid, and al-Farra' chose it.

On this view, the Qur'an was called "najm" because it was scattered in its revelation, and the Arabs call dispersal "tanjīm" and what is dispersed "najm"; and the "nujūm" of a book are its portions. One says, "I made my money owed by so-and-so in installments (nujūman munajjamah), each installment such-and-such." The origin of this is that the Arabs used the risings of the moon and its settings as appointed times for the due dates of their debts and terms. So they say, "When the star rises," meaning the Pleiades, "the debt is due to you." From this is the saying of Zuhayr about a blood-money (diyah) that was made payable in installments on the one liable:

They pay it in installments, one people to another, as a fine,
and they have not shed between them a full brimming measure [of blood].

Then every payment in installments came to be called "tanjīm" (dispersal), even if it was not fixed by the rising of a star.

As for His saying "hawā" (set/fell) on this view: it means it descended from above to below. Abu Zayd said: "The eagle hawat" (falls) "tahwī hawan," with the ha' pronounced with a fatḥah, when it swoops down upon prey or other things. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said likewise, and he distinguished between "al-hawā" (with fatḥah, the act of falling) and "al-hawā" in the line:

"And the bucket, in its ascent, is quick in its descent..."

Al-Layth said: The common people say "al-hawā" with ḍammah as the verbal noun of "hawā yahwā," and likewise al-Aṣmaʿi said: "hawā yahwā," with fatḥah on the ha', is when something falls downward. He said: and likewise "al-hawy" in travel, when it proceeds.

Here there is a matter that must be pointed out, in which Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm committed the most grievous error. He mentioned among the names of the Lord, exalted is He, "al-Hawā" with fatḥah on the ha', and he argued by what is in the Sahih from the hadith of ʿAʾisha that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say in his prostration, "Subhana Rabbiya al-Aʿla" (Glory be to my Lord, the Most High). Abu Muhammad thought that "al-Hawā" is an attribute of the Lord. This is one of his errors, may Allah have mercy on him. Rather, "al-Hawā," on the pattern of faʿīl, is the name for a portion of the night; it is said, "a hawā of the night has passed," on the pattern of faʿīl, just as "a hazīʿ of it has passed," meaning an edge and a side of it. He used to say "Subhana Rabbiya al-Aʿla" in a portion of the night and a side of it. And I have made this explicit in the other wording, where she said: "He used to say, 'Subhana Rabbiya al-Aʿla,' al-Hawā of the night."

We return to His saying ﴿By the star when it sets﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said, in the narration of ʿAli ibn Abi Talha and ʿAtiyya: it means the Pleiades when they fall and set, and this is the other narration from Mujahid. When the Arabs say "al-najm" without qualification, they mean the Pleiades. [A poet] said: "So she remained counting the stars (al-najm)."

Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: it means the stars when they are scattered on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn ʿAbbas, in the narration of ʿIkrima, said: it means the stars by which the devils are pelted when they fall in their wake at the time of eavesdropping.

This is the view of al-Hasan, and it is the most apparent of the opinions. Allah, glorified be He, has sworn by this manifest, observed sign which Allah set up as a sign and as a protection of the revelation from the devils' eavesdropping on it, to show that what His Messenger brought is truth and sincerity, and that Satan has no path or way to it. Rather, by the star when it sets, a watch has been kept, as an observer before the revelation and a guard for it.

On this view, the connection between the thing sworn by and the thing sworn to is most evident, and in what is sworn by there is evidence for what is sworn to.

It is not clear that the Qur'an at its revelation is called "the star when it sets," nor that its revelation is called "falling," and the Qur'an has no precedent for this, so this word should not be read in that sense. Nor is it clear that this oath is restricted to the Pleiades alone when they set; nor is it clear either that the oath is by the stars when they are scattered on the Day of Resurrection. Rather, that is something the Lord swears to and establishes by His signs. He does not make Himself the proof of it, since it is not evident to the addressees, especially those who deny the Resurrection. For He, glorified be He, argues only from what cannot be denied or contested. So the strongest opinion is the view of al-Hasan, and Allah knows best.

There is a connection between the thing sworn by and the thing sworn to that is not hidden: the stars by which the devils are pelted are among the signs of Allah, by which He protects His religion and His revelation, and His signs sent down upon His Messenger, through which His religion, His law, His names and His attributes have become manifest. These observed stars were made servants and guards for those revelations, and He, glorified be He, negated from His Messenger error, which contradicts guidance, and deviation, which contradicts rectitude. Within this negation is the testimony that he is upon guidance and rectitude. Guidance is in his knowledge, and rectitude is in his intention; these two foundations are the ultimate perfection of the servant, and by them is his happiness and success. By them the Prophet described his successors when he said: "Upon you is my sunnah and the sunnah of the rightly-guided caliphs after me."

Thus al-rāshid is the opposite of al-ghāwī, and al-mahdī is the opposite of al-ḍāll. He is the one whose soul has been purified by beneficial knowledge and righteous action, and he is the possessor of guidance and the religion of truth. The rightly-guided one is not confused with the misguided, deviant one except by the most ignorant of Allah's creatures, the most blind in heart, and the furthest from the reality of humanity.

How fine is the saying of the poet:

"What benefit is sight to the brother of this world when light and darkness are alike to him?"

So people are of four kinds: one who is astray in his knowledge and deviant in his intention and knowledge; these are the worst of creation, and they are the opponents of the messengers.

The second is one who is guided in his knowledge but deviant in his intention and action; these are the "angry" people (al-umma al-ghaḍabiyya) and whoever imitates them, and this is the state of everyone who knows the truth but does not act upon it.

The third is one who is astray in his knowledge but whose intention is good, while he is unaware.

The fourth is one who is guided in his knowledge and rightly directed in his intention; these are the heirs of the prophets. Though they are fewest in number, they are the most honoured in rank with Allah; they are the elect of Allah among His servants and the party of Allah among His creation.

Consider how He, glorified be He, said ﴿your companion﴾ and did not say "Muhammad," as an emphasis on establishing the proof against them, that he is their companion, and they know him best, his condition, his sayings and his deeds, and that they do not know him to have lied, nor to have deviated, nor to have erred, and they do not find fault with him in a single matter ever. He drew attention to this meaning with His saying ﴿Did they not recognize their Messenger?﴾ and His saying ﴿Your companion is not a madman﴾.

(Chapter)

Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is not but a revelation that is revealed﴾

He (Allah) exonerates the speech of His Messenger from proceeding from desire, and by this perfection He guided him and gave him right direction.

He said ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ and did not say "he does not speak with desire," because his speaking "from desire" is more eloquent, for it implies that his speech does not proceed from desire.

And if it does not proceed from desire, how could he speak by it?

Thus the negation of both matters includes the negation of desire from the source of speech and its negation from himself; so his speech is with truth, and its source is guidance and right direction, not error and misguidance.

Then He said ﴿It is not but a revelation that is revealed﴾. He returned the pronoun to the source understood from the verb, meaning: his speech is nothing but revelation that is revealed. This is better than the view of those who make the pronoun refer to the Qur'an, for that would restrict his speech to the Qur'an, whereas the Sunnah is also revelation that is revealed.

Al-Shafi'i argued for this, saying: Perhaps the proof of the one who holds this view is His saying ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and the wisdom﴾.

He said: Perhaps his proof is that the Messenger of Allah said to the father of the man who committed adultery with the wife of the other man, the one who made peace with him over the sheep and the servant:

"By Him in whose hand my soul is, I will certainly judge between you both by the Book of Allah. The sheep and the servant are returned to you..." — the hadith.

In the two Sahihs, Ya'la ibn Umayyah used to say to Umar, "I wish I could see the Messenger of Allah when revelation descends upon him." Then when he was at al-Ji'ranah, a man asked him, "What do you think of a man who entered into ihram for umrah while wearing a robe after being perfumed with saffron?" The Prophet looked at him for a while and then remained silent. Then revelation came, and Umar gestured with his hand to Ya'la, and he came and put his head in, and there was the Prophet (ﷺ) in ihram, snoring. Then it was lifted from him.

He said, "Where is the one who asked just now?"

So the man was brought, and he said, "Take off the robe, wash off the trace of the perfume, and do in your umrah what you do in your hajj."

Al-Shafi'i said: Muslim informed us from Ibn Jurayj from Abu Tawus from his father that he [the Prophet] had a book which revelation had brought, and what the Messenger of Allah prescribed of charity and blood-money came only by revelation.

Al-Awza'i mentioned from Hassan ibn 'Atiyyah, who said:

Jibril used to descend upon the Messenger of Allah with the Sunnah just as he descended upon him with the Qur'an, teaching him it.

Al-Awza'i also mentioned from Abu 'Ubayd, the companion of Sulayman, who said: Al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah informed me, Ibn Fudaylah narrated to me, he said:

It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Set prices for us." He said: "Allah will not question me about a practice I introduce among you that He did not command me to do; rather, ask Allah for His bounty."

This "Ibn Nadlah" is called Talhah.

It is authentically related from him that he said: "Indeed I have been given the Book and its like along with it."

This is undoubtedly the Sunnah, and Allah the Exalted said ﴿And Allah sent down to you the Book and the wisdom﴾, and they are the Qur'an and the Sunnah. And success is from Allah.

(Section)

Then Allah, exalted is He, informs about the attribute of the one who taught him the revelation and the Qur'an, which is known to be the opposite of the attributes of the devil, the teacher of misguidance and error. So He says: ﴿He has been taught by one mighty in power﴾.

This is similar to His saying: ﴿Possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne, secure﴾. We have mentioned there the reason for describing him with power.

And His saying ﴿Possessor of strength (mirrah)﴾ means: beautiful in appearance, fine in form, possessing majesty. He is not a devil, the ugliest and most deformed of Allah's creation, but rather he is among the most beautiful of creation, the strongest, and the greatest in trustworthiness and rank with Allah. This is a vindication of the bearer of the revelation and prophethood and a praise of him, as its parallel was mentioned in Surah al-Takwir. Thus He describes him with knowledge, power, beauty of appearance, and majesty. These were the attributes of the human and angelic Messenger, so the Messenger of Allah was the bravest, most knowledgeable, most beautiful, and most dignified of people. The devils and their students are the opposite of that: they are the ugliest of creation in form and meaning, and the most ignorant of creation, the weakest in resolve and souls.

(Benefit)

Ibn al-Qayyim said in (al-Sawa'iq al-Mursalah):

Al-mirrah is the radiant, beautiful appearance. So He gave him complete strength within and beauty of appearance without. These two perfections are what the wife of the governor showed to the women who blamed her regarding her love for Yusuf, for she seated them in the house, ﴿and she said: "Come out before them." So when they saw him, they magnified him and cut their hands and said: "Allah forbid! This is not a human. This is none but a noble angel."﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. So she informed them that his inward was better and more beautiful.

﴿She said: "That is the one you blamed me for. I did seek to seduce him, but he refrained."﴾ [Yusuf: 32]. So she showed them his outward beauty and informed them of his inward beauty.

(Section)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Possessor of strength, so he stood firm﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Possessor of a good appearance."

Qatadah said: "Possessor of good form."

Ibn Jarir said: "By mirrah is meant the soundness of the body and its freedom from defects and afflictions; when a human body is like that, it is strong."

Mirrah is the singular of mirar, and what is intended is "possessor of sound strength." From it is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family: "Charity is not lawful for the rich, nor for one possessing sound strength (dhi mirrah sawi)."

I say: This is the proof of those who said that mirrah means strength in the verse, and this is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

However, this is a weak view, because He had already described him as ﴿Mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5] before that.

There is no doubt that mirrah in the hadith means strength, not a fine appearance.

So either it may be said that mirrah is used for both meanings, or it may be said — and this is the more apparent — that mirrah is soundness and freedom from outward and inward defects and afflictions, and this necessarily entails perfection and beauty of creation.

For defect and affliction only arise from weakness of creation and composition, so it is strength and soundness that includes beauty and goodness. And Allah knows best.

Then He mentioned the rising of this teacher on the highest horizon, his approach, his descent and his nearness to the Messenger of Allah, and Allah's revelation of what He revealed. Subhanahu depicted for the people of faith the picture of the situation of Gabriel's descent from Him until he rose on the horizon, then drew near, descended, and came close to His Messenger, and revealed to him what Allah commanded him to reveal, as if they were witnessing the scene and seeing it: descending from the sky until he stood on the highest horizon, then came down and drew near to Muhammad and addressed him with what Allah commanded, saying: "Your Lord says to you such and such." He, Glorified is He, informed about the distance of this nearness, that it was "the measure of two bow-lengths or nearer," and this is not by way of doubt but a confirmation of the measure of the distance, that it does not exceed two bow-lengths at all, just as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾, a confirmation of this number, that they are not fewer than a hundred thousand men. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones or even harder in hardness﴾, meaning their hardness is not less than the hardness of stones; rather, if it does not exceed the hardness of stones, it is not below it.

This meaning is better, more subtle, and more precise than the view of those who make "aw" in these places mean "bal" (rather), and the view of those who make it indicate doubt in relation to the speaker's opinion, and the view of those who make it mean "wa" (and). So reflect upon it. End.

(Section)

Then Allah, exalted is He, informs about the attribute of the one who taught him the revelation and the Qur'an, which is known to be the opposite of the attributes of the devil, the teacher of misguidance and error. So He says: ﴿He has been taught by one mighty in power﴾.

This is similar to His saying: ﴿Possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne, secure﴾. We have mentioned there the reason for describing him with power.

And His saying ﴿Possessor of strength (mirrah)﴾ means: beautiful in appearance, fine in form, possessing majesty. He is not a devil, the ugliest and most deformed of Allah's creation, but rather he is among the most beautiful of creation, the strongest, and the greatest in trustworthiness and rank with Allah. This is a vindication of the bearer of the revelation and prophethood and a praise of him, as its parallel was mentioned in Surah al-Takwir. Thus He describes him with knowledge, power, beauty of appearance, and majesty. These were the attributes of the human and angelic Messenger, so the Messenger of Allah was the bravest, most knowledgeable, most beautiful, and most dignified of people. The devils and their students are the opposite of that: they are the ugliest of creation in form and meaning, and the most ignorant of creation, the weakest in resolve and souls.

(Benefit)

Ibn al-Qayyim said in (al-Sawa'iq al-Mursalah):

Al-mirrah is the radiant, beautiful appearance. So He gave him complete strength within and beauty of appearance without. These two perfections are what the wife of the governor showed to the women who blamed her regarding her love for Yusuf, for she seated them in the house, ﴿and she said: "Come out before them." So when they saw him, they magnified him and cut their hands and said: "Allah forbid! This is not a human. This is none but a noble angel."﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. So she informed them that his inward was better and more beautiful.

﴿She said: "That is the one you blamed me for. I did seek to seduce him, but he refrained."﴾ [Yusuf: 32]. So she showed them his outward beauty and informed them of his inward beauty.

(Section)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Possessor of strength, so he stood firm﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Possessor of a good appearance."

Qatadah said: "Possessor of good form."

Ibn Jarir said: "By mirrah is meant the soundness of the body and its freedom from defects and afflictions; when a human body is like that, it is strong."

Mirrah is the singular of mirar, and what is intended is "possessor of sound strength." From it is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family: "Charity is not lawful for the rich, nor for one possessing sound strength (dhi mirrah sawi)."

I say: This is the proof of those who said that mirrah means strength in the verse, and this is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

However, this is a weak view, because He had already described him as ﴿Mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5] before that.

There is no doubt that mirrah in the hadith means strength, not a fine appearance.

So either it may be said that mirrah is used for both meanings, or it may be said — and this is the more apparent — that mirrah is soundness and freedom from outward and inward defects and afflictions, and this necessarily entails perfection and beauty of creation.

For defect and affliction only arise from weakness of creation and composition, so it is strength and soundness that includes beauty and goodness. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 53, verse 8:

As for His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat al-Najm: ﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾

It is other than the drawing near and descent in the story of the Night Journey (al-Isra'). What is meant in (Surat al-Najm) is the drawing near and descent of Jibril (Gabriel), as ʿA'isha and Ibn Mas'ud said. The context also indicates this, for He said: ﴿Taught by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5], and this is Jibril: ﴿Possessed of strength; then he stood firm, while he was on the highest horizon. Then he drew near and came down﴾ [al-Najm: 6-8].

So all the pronouns refer back to this mighty teacher, who is ﴿possessed of strength﴾, meaning power (quwwa). He is the one who ﴿stood firm on the highest horizon﴾, and he is the one who ﴿drew near and came down﴾, so that there was between Muhammad (ﷺ) a distance of ﴿two bow-lengths or nearer﴾. As for the drawing near and descent in the hadith of the Night Journey, that is explicit that it is the drawing near and descent of the Lord, blessed and exalted. There is no reference in (Surat al-Najm) to that. Rather, in it is that he saw him another time ﴿near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 13-14]. This is Jibril, whom Muhammad (ﷺ) saw in his own form twice: once on the earth, and once near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

The author of al-Manazil (the Shaykh, Abu Isma'il al-Ansari) said, in the chapter on "Connection" (bab al-ittisal): Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then he drew near and came down. And was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ [al-Najm: 8-9].

He despaired the intellects, and he cut off inquiry with his saying: "or nearer."

It seems the Shaykh understood from the verse that the one who drew near and came down, so that there was between Muhammad (ﷺ) a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer, is Allah, mighty and majestic.

Although a group of the exegetes said this, the correct view is that it is Jibril, upon him be prayers and peace. He is the one described by what was mentioned from the beginning of the surah up to His saying: ﴿And he saw him another time, near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 13-14].

Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it in the authentic hadith. ʿA'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

"I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this verse. He said: 'It is Jibril. I did not see him in the form in which he was created except twice.'"

The wording of the Qur'an does not indicate anything other than this, from several aspects.

The first: He said ﴿Taught by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5].

This is Jibril, whom Allah described as possessing power in Surat al-Takwir, when He said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessed of power, esteemed with the Lord of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 19-20].

The second: He said ﴿possessed of strength﴾ [al-Najm: 6], meaning good character, and this is the noble one mentioned in al-Takwir.

The third: He said ﴿Then he stood firm, while he was on the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 6-7].

This is the side of the highest heaven. This is Jibril's standing on the highest horizon. As for the standing of the Lord, majestic is His majesty, it is upon His Throne.

The fourth: He said ﴿Then he drew near and came down. And was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ [al-Najm: 8-9].

This is the drawing near and descent of Jibril to the earth, where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was. As for the drawing near and descent in the hadith of the Mi'raj (Ascension), the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was above the heavens. There the Almighty, majestic is His majesty, drew near to him and descended..

So the drawing near and descent in the hadith is other than the drawing near and descent in the verse, even if they agree in wording.

The fifth: He said ﴿And he saw him another time, near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 13-14]. The one seen near the Lote-tree is definitely Jibril, and the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it this way, when he said to ʿA'isha: "That was Jibril."

The sixth: The referent of the pronoun in His saying ﴿And he saw him﴾ [al-Najm: 13], and in His saying ﴿Then he drew near﴾ [al-Najm: 8], and in His saying "stood firm," and in His saying ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 7], is one and the same. It is not permissible to differ between the referent and what is referred to without evidence.

The seventh: He, glorified be He, mentioned in this surah the two noble messengers: the angelic one and the human one. He declared the human one free from error and deviation, and He declared the angelic one free from being an ugly, weak devil. Rather, he is strong, noble, and of good character. This is the same as the description mentioned in Surat al-Takwir.

The eighth: He informed there that he saw him on the clear horizon (al-ufuq al-mubin), and here He informed that he saw him on the highest horizon (al-ufuq al-a'la). It is one and the same, described with two attributes: he is clear, and he is high, for whenever a thing rises, it becomes evident and appears.

The ninth: He said ﴿possessed of strength﴾ [al-Najm: 6], and strength (mirra) is firm good character. So He informed about the good character of the one who taught the Prophet (ﷺ), then He related the whole report about him in one sequence.

The tenth: If it were a report about the Lord, may He be exalted, the Qur'an would have indicated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord, glorified be He, twice: once on the horizon, and once near the Lote-tree. It is known that if the matter were like this, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have said to Abu Dharr when he asked him:

"Did you see your Lord? He said: 'Light; how could I see Him?'"

So how would the Qur'an inform that he saw Him twice, and then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "How could I see Him?"

This is more emphatic than his saying "I did not see Him," because a negation accompanied by a statement implies only the report of the absence of vision, whereas this includes negation and a measure of denial directed at the questioner, as when you say to a man: "Did such-and-such happen?" and he replies: "How could that be?"

The eleventh: No mention of the Lord, majestic is His majesty, preceded, to which the pronoun in His saying ﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾ [al-Najm: 8] could refer.

What the pronoun refers back to is not suitable for Him. Rather, it refers to His servant.

The twelfth: How can a pronoun refer to something that was not mentioned, while its reference to what was mentioned is left aside even though that is more appropriate for it?

The thirteenth: The mention of "your companion" (sahibukum) has already preceded, and He referred to him with the pronouns that befit him. Then after him He mentioned "mighty in power, possessed of strength," and He referred to him with the pronouns that befit him. The whole report is about these two referents, namely the angelic messenger and the human messenger.

The fourteenth: He, glorified be He, informed that this one who drew near and came down was on the highest horizon, which is the horizon of the heaven. Rather, he was beneath it, having drawn near to the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds (ﷺ). But the drawing near and descent of the Lord, may He be exalted, according to what is in the hadith of Sharik, was from above the Throne, not to the earth.

The fifteenth: They did not dispute with him, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, about the vision of his Lord, nor did he inform them of it, for their dispute with him about it to occur. Rather, they disputed with him about the seeing of the signs that he informed them of, which Allah had shown him. Had the Lord, may He be exalted, informed them, their dispute with him about it would have been greater than their dispute about seeing the created things.

The sixteenth: He, glorified be He, affirmed the correctness of what the Messenger (ﷺ) saw, and that their dispute with him about that is false, by His saying: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18]. If the one seen had been the Lord, glorified and exalted be He, and the dispute about it came from them, then the confirmation of that vision would have been more fitting, and the context would have required it more. And Allah knows best.

**Chapter on Unveiling (al-Mukashafa)**

The author of *al-Manazil* said:

"Chapter on Unveiling (al-Mukashafa). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾."

The way he argues from the indication of the verse is this: Allah, glory be to Him, unveiled to His servant (ﷺ) what He had not unveiled to anyone else, and gave him knowledge of what He had not given to anyone else. Thus his noble heart received, through the unveiling of realities that never occur to anyone else's mind, what Allah specially granted him. Revelation (al-iyha') is swift and hidden notification, from which comes the saying "al-wahā al-wahā," meaning: hurry, hurry.

His words "what He revealed" are vague because of its magnitude, for vagueness is sometimes used to express grandeur. A parallel is the Exalted's words: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78]. That is, a great matter beyond description.

The Shaykh said: Unveiling has three degrees.

The first degree is an unveiling that indicates sound verification. It is not continuous. It comes at some times and not others, and no dispersion opposes it. Yet the ghayn (a veil of heedlessness) may sometimes cloud his state, although he has reached a level where no interruption diverts him, no cause turns him away, and no portion of worldly gain cuts him off. This is the degree of the seeker (al-qasid). If it becomes continuous, it is the second degree.

Sound unveiling consists of knowledge that the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted, produces in the heart of the servant, and by which He informs him of matters hidden from others. Sometimes He sustains it, and sometimes He withholds it from him through heedlessness of it, and conceals it from him by the ghayn that covers his heart, which is the finest of veils, or by the cloud (al-ghaym), which is coarser than it, or by the ran (rust), which is the most severe of them.

The first occurs to the prophets, peace be upon them, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, there is a veil (ghayn) over my heart, and I seek forgiveness from Allah more than seventy times a day."

The second occurs to the believers. The third belongs to those upon whom wretchedness has prevailed. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿No! Rather, what they used to earn has become rust upon their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 14]. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: It is sin after sin that covers the heart until it becomes like rust upon it.

The veils are ten.

The first is the veil of ta'til (denial), which is the negation of the realities of the Names and Attributes. It is the coarsest of them. For the one under this veil it is not possible to know Allah, nor to reach Him at all, any more than it is possible for a stone to ascend upward.

The second is the veil of shirk, which is that the heart worships other than Allah.

The third is the veil of verbal innovation (bid'a qawliyya), like the veil of the people of desires and corrupt doctrines, whatever their differences.

The fourth is the veil of practical innovation (bid'a 'amaliyya), like the veil of innovating practitioners of the path (ahl al-suluk) in their way and conduct.

The fifth is the veil of the people of hidden major sins, like the veil of those possessed by arrogance, self-admiration, showing off, envy, boasting, vanity, and the like.

The sixth is the veil of the people of manifest major sins. Their veil is thinner than that of their brethren among the people of hidden major sins, despite their abundance of worship, asceticism, and striving. The major sins of these people are closer to repentance than the major sins of those others, for they have become stations for them, which they do not shy from displaying and bringing forth in the forms of worship and knowledge. So the people of manifest major sins are nearer to safety than they are.

And their hearts are better than their hearts.

The seventh is the veil of the people of minor sins.

The eighth is the veil of the people of excess and of indulgence in permissible things.

The ninth is the veil of those heedless of recalling what they were created for and what is required of them, and of what Allah requires of them in continual remembrance, gratitude, and worship.

The tenth is the veil of the striving seekers, who exert themselves in the journey away from the goal.

These are ten veils between the heart and Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, which stand between it and this matter. These veils arise from four elements: the element of the self (nafs), the element of Satan, the element of the world (dunya), and the element of desire (hawa). It is absolutely impossible to lift these veils while their roots and elements remain in the heart.

These four elements corrupt speech, action, intention, and the path, according to their dominance and their weakness. They cut off the road of speech, action, and intention from reaching the heart. And whatever reaches the heart of it, they cut off for it the road to reaching the Lord. Between speech and action and the heart there is a distance over which the servant travels to his heart in order to see its wonders. In this distance are the highwaymen mentioned. If he fights them and the action reaches his heart, it circulates in it and seeks passage from there to Allah, for it does not settle short of arriving at Him: ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality﴾ [al-Najm: 42]. When it reaches Allah, glory be to Him, He rewards it with an increase in his faith, certainty, knowledge, and intellect, and beautifies by it his outward and inward being. He guides him by it to the best of characters and deeds, and turns away from him by it the worst of characters and deeds. Allah, glory be to Him, raises up from that action for the heart an army with which it fights the highwaymen who block the way to Him. It fights the world by renunciation of it and by removing it from the heart, and it does not harm him that it is in his hand and his house, nor does that prevent the strength of his certainty in the Hereafter. It fights Satan by refusing to respond to the call of desire, for Satan does not leave desire. It fights desire by submitting the matter absolutely and standing with it, such that no desire remains in him regarding what he does and what he leaves. And it fights the self (nafs) by the strength of sincerity.

All of this is when the action finds an outlet from the heart to the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted. But if it circulates within it and finds no outlet, and the self prevails over it, seizes it, and makes it an army for itself, then it springs upon him with it, rises, and transgresses. You see him at his most ascetic, his most devoted in worship, and his most diligent, yet he is at his farthest from Allah. The people of major sins are closer to Allah in their hearts than he is, and nearer than he is to sincerity and deliverance.

Look at the devout, constant worshipper, the ascetic, on whose forehead is the mark of prostration: how the transgression of his action led him to deny the Prophet (ﷺ), and led his companions to despise the Muslims, until they drew their swords against them and made their blood lawful.

And look at the habitual drinker, the drunkard, who was often brought to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he would apply the prescribed punishment for drinking: how the strength of his faith, certainty, love of Allah and His Messenger, and his humility and submission before Allah stood by him, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade cursing him.

From this it becomes clear that the transgression of sins is safer in its outcome than the transgression of acts of obedience.

Imam Ahmad narrated in *Kitab al-Zuhd* that Allah, glory be to Him, revealed to Musa (ﷺ): "O Musa, warn the sincere (siddiqin), for I do not place My justice upon anyone without punishing him, without wronging him. And give glad tidings to the sinners, for no sin is too great for Me to forgive."

(Section)

Then He, exalted is He, informs of the heart's confirmation of what the eyes saw, and that the heart affirmed the eye. It is not like one who saw something other than it really is, so his heart denied what his sight showed him; rather, what he saw with his sight, his heart confirmed, and he knew that it was so. There are two readings concerning it: one with the lightened form of kadhdhaba (kaddhaba, lightened), and the other with its doubled form (kadhdhaba, intensified). It is said: "his eye deceived him" (kadhdhabathu ʿaynuhu), "his heart deceived him" (kadhdhabahu qalbuhu), and "his body deceived him" (kadhdhabahu jasaduhu), when it failed what he assumed and conjectured.

The poet said:

"Did your eye deceive you, or did you see in Wasit, in the dark of night, the phantom of al-Rabab?"

That is, it showed you what has no reality. So He negated this from His Messenger, and informed him that his heart did not deny what he saw.

The "mā" (what) may be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), so the meaning is: his heart did not deny his seeing.

Or it may be a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), so the meaning is: the heart did not deny that which his eye saw.

On both assessments, it is an information about the agreement of the heart's seeing with the eye's seeing, their conformity, and the confirmation of each of them by the other.

This is quite evident in the doubled reading. A group of scholars, among them al-Mubarrad, found it problematic, and he said regarding this reading: "Because if he saw with his heart, then he also knew it with his heart, and when knowledge occurs there is no denial with it, for if a thing is known in the heart, how can denial accompany it?"

I say: The answer to this has two aspects:

The first: a man may imagine a thing contrary to what it is, so his heart denies it, since it shows him the image of the known thing contrary to what it is, just as his eye denies it. Thus one says: "his heart denied him," "his assumption denied him," and "his eye denied him." So He, glory be to Him, negated this from His Messenger and informed that what the heart saw was just as it saw it, like one who sees a thing according to its true reality; it is correct to say: "his eye did not deny it."

The second: that the pronoun in "ra'ā" (he saw) refers to the seeing (al-ra'y), not to the heart, so the meaning is: the heart did not deny what the eye saw.

This, praise be to God, has no difficulty in it. The meaning is: the heart did not deny what the eye saw, rather it confirmed it, and this holds for both readings.

So the meaning is: the heart did not make him imagine that he saw when he had not seen, nor did it accuse his sight.

Then He, glory be to Him, rebuked them for their obstinate denial and their rejection of what he saw, just as one rebukes an ignorant person for being obstinate toward a scholar and disputing with him about what the scholar has done. There are two readings: ﴿Afatumārūnahu﴾ and ﴿Afatumrūnahu﴾. This mirā' (disputing) originally derives from denial and repulsion; one says "mariytu al-rajul ḥaqqahu" (I denied the man his right) when one has rejected it.

As the poet said:

"If you have forsaken a brother of truth and nobility, indeed you have denied a brother who never denied you."

From this comes al-mumārāh, which is contention and obstinacy. For this reason the verb is followed by ʿalā (on), and it keeps its own sense and is not in the sense of ʿan (from), as al-Mubarrad said; rather the verb implies the meaning of obstinacy.

This is clearer in the reading with the alif. Abū ʿUbaydah preferred the reading of the one who reads ﴿Afatumrūnahu﴾. He said: "This is because the polytheists' concern was only denial of the revelation that came to them, and this was more common among them than disputation." That is, whoever reads ﴿Afatumārūnahu﴾ means "Will you dispute with him?", and whoever reads ﴿Afatumrūnahu﴾ means "Will you deny him?" Their denial of what he brought was their characteristic, and it was more prevalent than their argument with him.

Abū ʿAlī and others disagreed and chose the reading ﴿Afatumārūnahu﴾. Abū ʿAlī said: "Whoever reads ﴿Afatumārūnahu﴾ means 'Will you dispute with him?' — a dispute by which you seek to repel him from what he knows and witnessed." The following verse strengthens this sense: ﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth after it has become clear﴾. Whoever reads ﴿Afatumrūnahu﴾ means "Will you deny him?" He said: "Disputation seems closer to this, because their denial occurred in this matter and in others, and the polytheists did dispute with him during the Isra'."

I say: The people combined disputation, repulsion and denial, so their disputation was a disputation of denial and repulsion, not a disputation of seeking guidance and clarification of the truth. The alif indicates disputation, and the use of ʿalā indicates obstinacy, so the reading with the alif encompasses both meanings together, and it is therefore preferable. And success is from God.

(Section)

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of His seeing (Jibril) a second time, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha).

The first time was below the heavens, at the high horizon, and the second was above the heavens, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary.

It is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he saw Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, in his own form in which he was created, twice. This is in the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim), from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who was asked about the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer﴾. He said: Ibn Mas'ud informed me that the Prophet saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings.

Also in the two Sahihs, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾, he said: He saw Jibril in his form, having six hundred wings.

Al-Bukhari also reported from him: He saw a green rafraf (a silken cushion or covering) that filled the horizon.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah regarding ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾, he said: He saw Jibril, peace be upon him.

Also in his Sahih, from Masruq, who said: I was reclining near Aishah, and she said: "Three things, whoever speaks of any one of them has greatly slandered Allah." I said: "What are they?" She said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has greatly slandered Allah."

He said: I was reclining, then I sat up and said: "O Mother of the Believers, give me time and do not hurry me. Did not Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, say ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾ and ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾?" She said: "I was the first of this Ummah to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and he said: 'It is only Jibril. I did not see him in his form in which he was created except these two times. I saw him descending from the sky, filling the vastness of his creation between the heaven and the earth.'" She said: "Did you not hear that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿No vision perceives Him, but He perceives [all] vision, and He is the Subtle, the Acquainted﴾? Did you not hear that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And it is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by inspiration or from behind a partition or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills. Indeed, He is Exalted and Wise﴾?"

She said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad concealed anything of the Book of Allah has greatly slandered Allah, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾."

She said: "Whoever claims that he knows what will happen tomorrow has greatly slandered Allah, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Say: No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾."

"And if Muhammad had concealed anything of what was revealed to him, he would have concealed this verse: ﴿And [remember] when you said to him on whom Allah bestowed favor and you bestowed favor, 'Keep your wife and fear Allah,' while you concealed within yourself that which Allah is to disclose, and you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾."

Also in the two Sahihs, from Masruq: I asked Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, "Did Muhammad see his Lord?" She said: "Glory be to Allah! My hair stood on end at what you said." In them also: I said to Aishah: "Then what about His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Then he approached and descended, and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer﴾?" She said: "That was only Jibril. He used to come to him in the form of men, but this time he came to him in his own form, which is his form, and he filled the horizon."

In Sahih Muslim, it is reported that Abu Dharr asked him: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "There is light; how could I see Him?"

Also in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us and spoke five words. He said:

"Indeed, Allah does not sleep, and it is not befitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light; if He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches."

This hadith was narrated by Muslim after the earlier hadith of Abu Dharr, and it serves as an explanation of it. This does not conflict with his saying in the Sahih hadith about the vision on the Day of Resurrection: "The veil will be lifted, and they will look at Him."

For the light that is the veil of the Lord, the Exalted, is meant the nearest veil to Him, which, if it were uncovered, nothing would be able to stand before it, as Ibn Abbas said regarding the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾. He said: "That is His light, which is His light; when He manifests with it, nothing can stand."

What Ibn Abbas mentioned requires that the words ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ are general and absolute, both in this world and the Hereafter. It does not follow from this that He is not seen; rather, He is seen in the Hereafter by sight without perception. If our eyes cannot withstand perceiving the sun as it is, even though they see it at the nearness that exists between creatures, then the gap between the eyes of creatures and the Essence of the Lord, the Majestic, is greater and greater still. For this reason, when the mountain received even a slight manifestation of the Lord's self-disclosure, it crumbled to dust and was broken apart by the glories of that measure of self-disclosure.

In the authentic marfu' hadith (traced to the Prophet):

"Two gardens of gold, their vessels and their adornments and what is in them, and two gardens of silver, their vessels and their adornments and what is in them. Between the people and their looking at their Lord there is nothing but the mantle of greatness upon His face in the Garden of Eden."

This indicates that the mantle of greatness upon His Face, blessed and exalted is He, is what prevents the vision of the Essence, but it does not prevent the vision itself. Greatness and majesty are a necessary attribute of His Essence, the Exalted. So when He manifests Himself to His servants on the Day of Resurrection and lifts the veil between them and Him, that is the created veil. As for the lights of the Essence, which veil one from perceiving it, these are attributes of the Essence that never separate from the Essence of the Lord, the Majestic. Had that veil been lifted, the glories of His Face would have burned away whatever of His creation His sight reached. This indication is sufficient in this matter for one who is sincere and certain.

As for the Jahmi mu'attil (a follower of Jahm ibn Safwan, who denied the divine attributes), all of this is false and impossible in his view.

The point is that the one reported as seen in Surah an-Najm is Jibril.

As for the statement of Ibn Abbas, "Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice," the apparent basis for it is this verse, but it has been clarified that what is seen in it is Jibril, so there is no evidence in it for what Ibn Abbas said. Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi reported a consensus on what Aishah said. In his refutation of Bishr al-Marisi, in discussing the hadith of Thawban and Mu'adh, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I saw my Lord last night in the best form," he related al-Marisi's false interpretation, then said: "Woe to you! The interpretation of this hadith is other than what you have taken. As for the Prophet's saying in the hadith of Abu Dharr, 'He did not see his Lord,' and the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) saying, 'You will not see your Lord until you die,' and Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, saying, 'Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has greatly slandered Allah,' and the Muslims have agreed upon that, along with the words of Allah: ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾." He means the vision of the people of this world. This vision was only in a dream. Seeing Allah is possible in every state, as is so. Mu'adh ibn Jabal narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I prayed what Allah willed of the night, then I lay down on my side, and my Lord came to me in the best form."

This is the interpretation of this hadith according to the scholars.

Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la thought that the reports from Imam Ahmad differed on whether the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), in three reports.

The first is that he saw Him. Al-Marwazi said: I said to Abu Abdullah (Ahmad): "They say that Aishah said, 'Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has greatly slandered Allah.' So with what can the saying of Aishah be countered?" He said: "With the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), 'I saw my Lord.'" The saying of the Prophet is greater than her saying.

He said: Al-Marwazi mentioned elsewhere that he said to Abu Abdullah: "Here is a man who says that Allah is seen in the Hereafter, but I do not say that Muhammad saw his Lord in this world." He became angry and said: "This is a matter that should be kept hidden. Accept the report as it came."

He said: The apparent meaning of this is that he affirmed a vision by the eye.

Harb transmitted: I said to Abu Abdullah: "Did the Prophet see his Lord in a dream, with his heart?" He said: The apparent meaning of this is the negation of vision. Likewise al-Athram transmitted, when he asked him about the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abis from the Prophet (ﷺ), "I saw my Lord in the best form." Ma'mar said it was confused, because Ma'mar narrated it from Ayyub, from Mu'bid, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abis, from the Prophet. Hammad narrated it from Qatadah, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas. Yusuf ibn Atiyyah narrated it from Qatadah, from Anas. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd narrated it from Jabir, from Khalid ibn al-Lajlaj, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abis, from a man among the Companions of the Prophet. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir narrated it from Ibn Abis, from Mu'adh, from the Prophet. The root of the hadith is one.

Al-Athram said: I said to Abu Abdullah, "Then what do you hold?" He said: Al-A'mash said, from Ziyad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Aliyah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart."

Al-Athram also transmitted that a man said to Ahmad, concerning al-Husayn al-Ashyab, that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not see his Lord, the Exalted." Someone objected to him and said: "Why do you say he saw Him, and do not say with his eye or with his heart, as the hadith came?" Al-Ashyab found this good, and Abu Abdullah said: "Good."

He said: The apparent meaning of this is the affirmation of a vision whose meaning one cannot grasp, whether it was with his eye or with his heart. These are the texts of Ahmad.

Al-Qadi considered them as differing and made the matter into three reports. Then he argued for the first report with the hadith of Umm al-Tufayl and the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abis al-Hadrami, but there is no evidence in them, because it was only a vision in a dream. He argued for it with something Ahmad would not have been pleased to cite, namely a hadith that is not authentic from Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah as marfu': "When the night of my Night Journey came, I saw my Lord in the best form, and He said: 'Over what do the highest assembly dispute?'" and he mentioned the hadith. This is definitely an error, for the story was in Medina, as Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was detained from us at the dawn prayer until we nearly saw the sun rising. Then he came out and prayed with us, and said: 'Last night I saw my Lord in the best form, and He said: "O Muhammad, over what do the highest assembly dispute?"'" and he mentioned the hadith.

So this took place in Medina, while the Night Journey took place in Mecca. There is no explicit text from Imam Ahmad or from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he saw Him with his eye while awake. Al-Qadi interpreted Ahmad's words in a way they cannot bear, and argued for what he understood from them with something that does not indicate it. Ahmad's words confirm one another, and the matter is one report from him, for he did not say "with his eye," but said "he saw," and followed in that the saying of Ibn Abbas, "Muhammad saw his Lord," and the wording of the hadith, "I saw my Lord," which is unrestricted, and its clarification has come in the other hadith.

However, Ahmad's rejection of Aishah's saying and his opposing it with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) indicates that he affirmed the vision which Aishah denied, since she did not deny a vision in a dream, and did not say, "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord in a dream has greatly slandered Allah."

This indicates one of two things:

Either Imam Ahmad rejected the saying of one who absolutely negated vision, since it contradicts the hadith.

Or it is a report from him affirming vision.

He explicitly said that he saw Him in a dream, with his heart, and this is a restriction on the vision. He affirmed that he saw Him absolutely, rejected the saying of one who negated vision altogether, and found good the saying of one who said "he saw Him, but not with his eye or with his heart." These texts from him agree with one another and do not contradict. How could Ahmad say "he saw Him with the eyes of his head while awake," when that has never come in any hadith? Ahmad only followed the wording of the hadith as it came. His rejection of the saying "he did not see Him at all" does not indicate an affirmation of a waking vision with the eye. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

Among what came in the hadith of the Mi'raj (Ascension):

"Then he was taken up that night from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to the lowest heaven. Jibril asked for it to be opened, and it was opened for him. There he saw Adam, the father of humanity, and he greeted him, and he returned the greeting, welcomed him, and acknowledged his prophethood. Allah showed him the souls of the blessed on his right and the souls of the wretched on his left. Then he was taken up to the second heaven, and asked for it to be opened, and there he saw Yahya ibn Zakariyya and Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus son of Mary). He met them and greeted them, and they returned his greeting, welcomed him, and acknowledged his prophethood. Then he was taken up to the third heaven, where he saw Yusuf, and he greeted him, and he returned his greeting, welcomed him, and acknowledged his prophethood. Then he was taken up to the fourth heaven, where he saw Idris, and he greeted him, and he welcomed him and acknowledged his prophethood. Then he was taken up to the fifth heaven, where he saw Harun ibn Imran, and he greeted him, and welcomed him and acknowledged his prophethood. Then he was taken up to the sixth heaven, where he met Musa ibn Imran, and he greeted him, and welcomed him and acknowledged his prophethood. When he passed him, Musa wept. He was asked: 'What makes you weep?' He said: 'I weep because a youth was sent after me, and more of his Ummah will enter the Garden than of my Ummah.' Then he was taken up to the seventh heaven, where he met Ibrahim, and he greeted him, welcomed him, and acknowledged his prophethood. Then he was lifted to Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary), then the Bayt al-Ma'mur (the frequented house) was raised for him. Then he was taken up to the Jabbar (the Compeller), the Majestic, and he drew near to Him until he was ﴿at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer﴾, so He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [An-Najm: 9]."

"And He prescribed upon him fifty prayers. He returned until he passed Musa, who said to him: 'With what were you commanded?' He said: 'With fifty prayers.' He said: 'Your Ummah cannot bear that. Return to your Lord and ask Him to lighten it for your Ummah.' He turned to Jibril as if consulting him about that, and he gestured: 'Yes, if you wish.' So Jibril raised him until he brought him to the Jabbar, blessed and exalted, and He was in His place." This is the wording of al-Bukhari in some of the chains. "He reduced ten for him. Then he descended until he passed Musa and informed him, and he said: 'Return to your Lord and ask Him to lighten it.' He kept going back and forth between Musa and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until He made them five. Then Musa commanded him to return and ask for lightening, and he said: 'I have become shy before my Lord, but I am content and submit.' When he had gone away, a caller called out: 'I have confirmed My obligation and lightened it for My servants.'"

The Companions differed on whether he saw his Lord that night or not.

It is authentically reported from Ibn Abbas that he saw his Lord, and it is authentically reported from him that he said: "He saw Him with his heart."

It is authentically reported from Aishah and Ibn Mas'ud that they denied that, and they said: "His saying, ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [An-Najm: 13], refers only to Jibril."

It is authentically reported from Abu Dharr that he asked him: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "There is light; how could I see Him?" That is: the light came between me and seeing Him, as he said in another wording: "I saw light."

Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi reported a consensus of the Companions that he did not see Him.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his soul, said: The saying of Ibn Abbas, "He saw Him," does not contradict this, nor does his saying, "He saw Him with his heart." It is authentically reported from him that he said: "I saw my Lord, blessed and exalted," but this was not during the Isra'; it was in Medina, when he was detained from them at the dawn prayer, and then he informed them about seeing his Lord, blessed and exalted, that night in his dream. On this Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, built his position, and he said: "Yes, he saw Him, truly, for the visions of the prophets are true, without doubt." But Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, did not say that he saw Him with the eyes of his head while awake. Whoever attributes that to him has erred about him. He said once: "He saw Him," and once: "He saw Him with his heart," so two reports were related from him, and a third was related from him through the alteration of some of his companions: that he saw Him with the eyes of his head. These texts of Ahmad exist, and there is nothing of that in them.

And as for Ibn ʿAbbas's statement that he saw Him with his heart twice: if his basis for it was the verse ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ [An-Najm: 11], and then the verse ﴿And he certainly saw Him in another descent﴾ [An-Najm: 13], then the apparent meaning is that this is his basis. For it is authentically reported from him (ﷺ) that this one seen was Jibril, whom he saw twice in his own form in which he was created. And this statement of Ibn ʿAbbas is the basis of Imam Ahmad's saying, "he saw Him with his heart," and Allah knows best.

(Section)

When He mentioned His seeing of Jibril at the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary (sidrat al-muntaha), He digressed from it and mentioned that the Garden of Refuge (jannat al-ma'wa) is near it, and that there covers it that which covers it of His command and creation. This is among the most excellent forms of digression, and it is a very subtle style in the Qur'an. It is of two kinds. The first is that one digresses from a thing to what is necessarily connected to it, like this, and like His saying: ﴿And if you ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they will surely say, "They were created by the Almighty, the All-Knowing."﴾ Then He digressed from their answer to His saying: ﴿He who made the earth for you a cradle and made for you therein roads that you may be guided, and who sends down from the sky water in measure, and We revive thereby a dead land. Thus you will be brought forth. And who created all the pairs and made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride, that you may sit firmly upon their backs.﴾

This is not part of their answer, but rather an affirmation of it and an establishment of proof against them.

Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Then who is the Lord of you both, O Moses?" He said, "Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided it." [Pharaoh] said, "Then what is the case of the former generations?" He said, "Knowledge of them is with my Lord in a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets."﴾

So this is Moses' answer, and then He, glorified is He, digressed from it to His saying: ﴿He who made for you the earth a cradle and threaded for you therein roads and sent down from the sky water, and We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants. Eat and graze your livestock. Indeed in that are signs for those of intellect. From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out once more.﴾ Then He returned to the speech from which He had digressed.

The second kind is digressing from the individual to the species, like His saying: ﴿And We had certainly created man from an extract of clay. Then We placed him as a sperm-drop in a firm place﴾ to its end. The first refers to Adam, and the second to his descendants.

(Section)

Al-ma'wa is a noun of place (mif'al) from awā, yaʼwī, meaning when one joins a place, arrives at it, and settles therein. Ata' reported from Ibn 'Abbas: it is the Garden to which Jibril and the angels retreat.

Mujahid and al-Kalbi said: it is the Garden to which the souls of the martyrs retreat.

Ka'b said: the Garden of Refuge is a garden in which there are green birds, in which the souls of the martyrs graze. 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) and Zirr ibn Hubaysh said: it is a garden among the gardens.

The correct view is that it is one of the names of Paradise, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿But as for one who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from [its] desire, then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.﴾

And He said concerning the Fire: ﴿Indeed, Hellfire will be [their] refuge﴾ and He said: ﴿And your refuge is the Fire.﴾

(Section)

On the words of the Exalted, ﴿Nor did his gaze swerve, nor did it transgress﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "His gaze did not swerve to the right or the left, nor did it exceed what he was commanded." This is also the view of the exegetes. Thus He negates for His Prophet what happens to the one who sees, who lacks courtesy in the presence of kings and great men: a glance to the right and to the left, and letting his eyes wander beyond what is before him.

And He informs of his perfect courtesy in that station and in that presence, for he did not turn to one side, nor did he extend his gaze to anything other than the signs he was shown and the wonders there. Rather, he stood in the position of a servant whose courtesy and lowered gaze and attention are fixed on what he was shown, without turning to anything else and without reaching for what he had not seen, along with the steadiness of heart and tranquility of the soul that this entails. This is the utmost perfection. Swerving of the gaze is turning it to the side, and its transgression is extending it forward to where it ends. Thus in this surah He has declared His knowledge free from error, His intention and action free from deviation, His speech free from desire, His heart free from denying what His sight saw, and His sight free from swerving and transgression. And thus is praise given:

"Those are noble deeds, not two bowls of milk mixed with water, which then became two bowls of urine."

(Benefit)

In the hadith of Ibn Masʿud concerning the words of the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾, he said: "He saw a green carpet which filled the horizon."

It is in the two Sahihs.

(Section)

Among the signs of love is lowering one's gaze when the beloved looks at him, and casting his eyes toward the ground, out of awe of him, shyness before him, and the greatness he holds in the heart. For this reason kings disapprove of one who addresses them while staring at them; rather, he keeps his gaze lowered to the ground. God the Exalted said, informing of the perfect courtesy of His Messenger on the night of the Isra': ﴿Nor did his gaze swerve, nor did it transgress﴾.

This is the utmost courtesy, for his gaze did not swerve to the right or the left, nor did it rise and reach beyond what it was seeing and attending to, as one who looks ahead to what lies beyond.

For this reason the Prophet ﷺ strongly forbade the worshipper to let his gaze wander toward the sky, and he warned them that their sight would be snatched away, because this is part of perfect courtesy toward the One before whom the worshipper stands. Rather, he should stand with head bowed and eyes lowered to the ground. And were it not that the greatness of the Lord of the worlds, glorified is He, is above His heavens on His Throne, there would be no difference between looking upward and looking downward.

[Section: Description of his courtesy ﷺ]

It is the custom of the people to mention in this context the words of the Exalted concerning His Prophet ﷺ, when He showed him what He showed him: ﴿Nor did his gaze swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17].

Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri opened the chapter on courtesy with this verse, and so did others.

It seems they had in mind the view of some of the exegetes that this is a description of his courtesy ﷺ in that station, in that he did not turn to one side and did not exceed what he saw. This is the perfection of courtesy. Its violation is for the beholder to turn to his right or left, or to look ahead beyond what is seen. Turning is swerving, and looking toward what lies ahead of what is seen is transgression and excess.

So the perfection of the beholder's attention to what is seen is that he does not divert his gaze from it to the right or the left, nor go beyond it.

This is the meaning I have gathered from Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God sanctify his spirit.

In this verse there are wondrous secrets, among the subtle matters of courtesy befitting the most perfect of mankind ﷺ: his sight and his insight were in harmony there; they agreed and bore witness together to what his sight beheld. Insight was in accord with it, and what his insight witnessed was also a truth seen by the sight. So the witnessing of sight and insight agreed in his case.

For this reason He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw. Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 11-12]

That is: the heart did not deny what it saw with the eye.

For this reason Abu Jaʿfar recited it: "ma kadhdhaba al-fu'adu ma ra'a" with the dhal shaddah, meaning the heart did not deny the sight; rather it confirmed it and was in accord with it, due to the soundness of the heart and the sight, or the rectitude of insight and sight, and the reality of what is seen by sight and insight being true.

The majority recited ﴿ma kadhaba al-fu'adu﴾ [al-Najm: 11] with the lighter form, which is transitive, and "ma ra'a" is its object: that is, his heart did not deny what his eyes saw; rather it was in accord with it and agreed with it.

So because his heart was in harmony with his outward form, his inward with his outward, and his sight with his insight, the heart did not lie about the sight.

The sight did not exceed its limit and so transgress; it did not turn from what was seen and so swerve. Rather the sight remained upright toward what was seen: it neither went beyond it nor inclined from it, just as the heart remained upright in turning to God and turning away from all else. For he turned to God with his whole self. The heart has swerving and transgression, and both were negated from his heart and sight. His heart did not swerve, turning away from God to other than Him, nor did it transgress by exceeding the station in which it was placed.

This is the utmost perfection and courtesy toward God, with which no other can be joined.

For it is the habit of souls, when placed in a lofty, exalted station, to look toward what is higher than it and above it. Do you not see that when Moses ﷺ was placed in the station of speaking and intimate converse, his soul longed for the vision? But when our Prophet ﷺ was placed in that station, he fulfilled its due; so why did neither his sight nor his heart turn to anything other than what he was placed in, in any way at all?

For this reason no obstacle hindered him, nor did any aim halt him, until he passed beyond the seven heavens, to the point that Moses reproached his Lord concerning him and said: "The children of Israel say: I am most honored in the sight of God. And this one has passed beyond me and left me behind in height. If only he were alone! But with him is his whole community." In the narration of al-Bukhari: "When I passed him, he wept. It was said: What makes you weep? He said: I weep because a youth sent after me will enter Paradise from his community in greater numbers than from mine." Then he passed beyond it in height, and no will hindered him, and no resolve held him back from the perfection of servanthood.

For this reason his mount in his night journey would outpace his stride with its gaze: it placed its foot at the farthest point of its sight, fitting the state of its rider and the vast distance of his course, which outstripped the whole world in its journey. So the hoof of al-Buraq did not differ from the place of his gaze.

Just as his foot ﷺ did not lag behind the place of his knowledge.

He ﷺ never ceased, in the advancing of his perfect courtesy with God, glorified is He, and in completing the stages of his servanthood to Him, until he broke through the veils of the heavens, and passed beyond the seven layers, and passed beyond the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and reached a station of nearness that outstripped the first and the last.

There the portions of nearness poured down upon him in full flow, and the clouds of veils dispersed from him, outwardly and inwardly, veil by veil.

He was placed in a station that the prophets and messengers envied. And when in the Hereafter he is placed in a second station of nearness, the first and the last will envy him for it. There he stood firm upon a straight path, from the perfection of his courtesy with God, and his gaze did not swerve from it nor transgress. Thus He established him in this world upon the most upright path of truth and guidance. And He swore by His speech to this in the Wise Reminder, saying, the Exalted: ﴿Ya Sin. By the Wise Qur'an. Indeed you are among the messengers, upon a straight path﴾ [Ya Sin: 1-4].

When the Day of Return comes, He will set him upon the Sirat, asking safety for his followers and the people of his sunnah, until they pass it into the Gardens of Bliss. That is the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills.

And God is the Owner of mighty bounty.

[Section: The station of resolve]

Among the stations of "﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾" is the station of resolve (himmah).

The author of Al-Manazil opened it with the words of the Exalted: ﴿Nor did his gaze swerve, nor did it transgress﴾.

It has already passed that he opened the chapter on courtesy with it, and we mentioned its reason.

As for the reason for opening "Resolve" with it: it indicates that his ﷺ resolve did not attach itself to anything other than what he witnessed and was placed in. Had his resolve gone beyond it, his gaze would have followed it.

Himmah (resolve) is a form from hamm (concern), which is the origin of will, but they reserved it for the culmination of will.

So hamm is its origin, and himmah is its end.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, say: In some divine reports, God the Exalted says: "I do not look at the words of the wise; I only look at his resolve."

He said: The common people say: The worth of every person is what he does well. The elite say: The worth of every person is what he seeks.

He meant: a person's worth is his resolve and his aim.

The author of Al-Manazil said:

Resolve (himmah) is that which takes possession of the launching toward the sought object, purely. Its possessor cannot contain it, nor turn away from it.

His saying "takes possession of the launching toward the sought object" means it dominates it as an owner dominates a possession; and "purely" means unmixed and pure.

The meaning is: when the servant's resolve attaches to the Real, the Exalted, with a sincere, pure, unmixed seeking.

That is the lofty resolve, which its possessor cannot contain, that is, cannot bear to delay, nor can he restrain himself, because of its overpowering dominion over him and the severity with which it compels him to seek the object, and he does not turn from it to anything other than its demands. The possessor of this resolve arrives swiftly and attains his sought object, so long as no obstacles hinder him and no attachments cut him off. And God knows best.

[Section: Degrees of resolve]

[The first degree: a resolve that guards the heart from the desolation of desire for the perishable]

Section

He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: a resolve that guards the heart from the desolation of desire for the perishing, leads it to desire what remains, and purifies it from the turbidity of slackness.

The perishing is this world and what is in it.

That is, the heart renounces it and its people.

He called desire for it "desolation" because it and its people make the hearts of those who desire it, and the hearts of those who renounce it, feel desolate.

As for those who desire it: their spirits and hearts are in desolation from their bodies, since what they were created for has escaped them, so they are desolate at its loss.

As for those who renounce it: they see it as desolate to them, because it stands between them and their sought object and beloved.

Nothing is more desolate to the heart than what stands between it and its sought object and beloved.

For this reason whoever contends with people for their wealth and seeks it from them is the most desolate and hateful thing to them.

Also: those who renounce it look at it only with insight, while those who desire it look at it with sight; so the renouncer finds desolate what the desirer finds pleasant.

As it is said:

"When the heart awakens and desire heals, the hearts see, though the eyes do not see."

Likewise this resolve leads him to desire what remains for its own sake, which is the Real, glorified is He.

What remains by His preserving is the Last Abode.

And it purifies him from the turbidity of slackness, that is, it frees and refines him from the filth of lethargy and slackness, which is the cause of waste and neglect. And God knows best.

[The second degree: a resolve that produces disdain for concern with secondary causes]

Section

He said: The second degree: a resolve that produces disdain for concern with secondary causes, and for descending to action, and for placing trust in hope.

The causes here are the causes of deeds, arising from seeing them, or seeing their fruits and wanting them, and the like, for these are, in their view, secondary causes.

The possessor of this resolve disdains, for his resolve and heart, to concern himself with secondary causes, for his resolve is above that.

So his concern with them and his thinking about them is a descent from the resolve.

And the absence of this concern is either because the causes have not come to him, since the height of his resolve has barred him from them, so he does not concern himself with what has not reached him; or because his resolve has encompassed his sought object, and his height comes upon those causes and uproots them. When he attaches his resolve to what is higher than them, the lofty resolve includes them, and their ruling is absorbed into the ruling of the lofty resolve.

This is a strange and very rare point. I do not know whether the Shaykh intended it or not.

As for his disdain for descending to action: this is a statement that requires qualification and clarification. The lofty of resolve has a goal above the goal of the workers and worshippers, and higher than it. He disdains to descend from the heaven of his lofty goal to mere action and worship, without journeying with the heart to God, so that it may be attained and he may win Him. For he is a seeker of his Lord, the Exalted, with a complete seeking in every meaning and consideration in his deeds, his worship and intimate converse, his sleep and waking, his movement and stillness, his solitude and mixing, and all his states. His heart has been dyed with turning to God, the Exalted, in the fullest dye.

This matter belongs only to the people of sincere love. They are not content with the mere forms of deeds, nor with confining seeking to the time of action alone.

As for his disdain for placing trust in hope: trust brings about lethargy and slackness. The possessor of this resolve is not among those people. How so? He is a flier, not a walker. And God knows best.
