**[Section: The second category, the people of ignorance and wrongdoing]**

**[The people of compound ignorance]**

**Section:**

The second category: the people of ignorance and wrongdoing, who combined ignorance of what was brought by the Messenger with wrongdoing through following their own desires. Concerning them Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They follow only conjecture and what their souls desire, though guidance has already come to them from their Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

These are of two kinds.

The first are those who think they are upon knowledge and guidance while they are in fact people of ignorance and error. These are the people of **compound ignorance** (al-jahl al-murakkab), who are ignorant of the truth, oppose it, and oppose its people, and who support falsehood and befriend it and its people. Yet they think they are upon something. ﴿Truly, they are the liars﴾. Because of their belief in something contrary to what it actually is, they are like the one who sees a mirage, which the thirsty man thinks is water, until when he reaches it he finds it to be nothing. Likewise, their deeds and their knowledge are like a mirage, which betrays its owner at the time he most needs it. And this is not merely a matter of disappointment and deprivation, as is the case of one who heads toward a mirage and finds no water. Rather, to this is added that he finds there the Most Wise of judges and the Most Just of the just, glory be to Him and exalted, who reckons for him what he had of knowledge and deed, and repays him in full, down to the weight of an atom. He then turns to the deeds he had done, hoping for their benefit, and makes them scattered dust, because they were not sincerely for His sake nor upon the sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ). And those false doubts which he used to imagine to be beneficial knowledge likewise become scattered dust. Thus his deeds and his knowledge become a source of regret for him.

The mirage (al-sarab) is what is seen in the vast open deserts, from the sunlight at midday, which flows over the surface of the earth as if it were running water. The qay'ah and the qa' are the flat land that has no mountain or valley in it. He has likened the knowledge and deeds of one who does not take his knowledge from revelation to a mirage that a traveler sees in the intense heat, so he heads toward it, his expectation is disappointed, and he finds it to be a blazing fire. Likewise, the knowledge and deeds of the people of falsehood, when people are gathered and thirst overcomes them, appear to them like a mirage, so they think it is water. But when they come to it, they find Allah there, and the angels of punishment seize them and drag them to the blazing Hellfire. They are given to drink boiling water which cuts their intestines. That water they are given is the very knowledge that does not benefit. And the deeds that were not for the sake of Allah the Exalted, Allah transforms into boiling water, which He gives them to drink. Likewise their food is of *dari'* (a bitter thorny plant), which neither nourishes nor relieves hunger. That is the knowledge and deeds of falsehood which they had in this world; likewise it neither nourishes nor relieves hunger. These are the ones concerning whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Shall we inform you of those who are the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 103]. They are the ones referred to in His saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. And they are the ones referred to in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets upon them, and they will not emerge from the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167].

The second kind of this category are the people of darknesses: those who are immersed in ignorance to such a degree that it has encompassed them from every side. They are like cattle, nay, they are even more astray in the way. Their deeds, which they performed without insight, but merely by blind imitation and following their forefathers, without a light from Allah the Exalted, are like *zulumat* (darknesses), the plural of *zulmah*. These darknesses are: the darkness of ignorance, the darkness of disbelief, the darkness of wrongdoing and following desire, the darkness of doubt and suspicion, and the darkness of turning away from the truth which Allah the Exalted sent His messengers with, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, and from the light which He sent down with them to bring people out of the darknesses into the light. For the one who turns away from what Allah the Exalted sent Muhammad (ﷺ) with, of guidance and the religion of truth, moves about within five darknesses: his speech is a darkness, his deed is a darkness, his entrance is a darkness, his exit is a darkness, and his destination is the darkness. His heart is dark, his face is dark, his speech is dark, and his condition is dark. When his owlish insight confronts the light which Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) with, he strives hard to flee from it, and its light almost snatches away his sight, so he flees into the darknesses of opinions, which are more suitable and fitting for him, as it has been said:

*Bats whom the daylight has blinded with its brightness,*
*and pieces of dark night have befriended them.*

So when he comes to the refuse of ideas and the shavings of minds, he roams and jumps about, displays and repeats, clatters and crackles. But when the light of revelation and the sun of messengership rises, he hides himself in the holes of insects.

(Section)

As for *al-lamam*, it is a fringe of madness. A man is called *malmum*, meaning he has *lamam*. It is also said: "a jinn touched (*lamma*) so-and-so," meaning he was possessed, or "a small amount," as al-Jawhari said. I say: the root of the word is closeness. From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾, and these are the minor sins.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said:
"I have seen nothing more similar to *lamam* than what Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'The eye commits adultery, and its adultery is the gaze. The hand commits adultery, and its adultery is the seizing. The foot commits adultery, and its adultery is walking. The private part commits adultery, and its adultery is the approach (*qubul*).'"

From the same root: *alamma bi-kadha*, meaning he approached it and drew near to it. A *ghulam mulimm* is a boy who is near puberty.

In a hadith: "Among what the spring produces is that which kills by bloating, or that which only approaches (*yulimm*)." That is, it comes close to that.

In sum, it is not clear that *lamam* is one of the names of love, though a group has mentioned this, unless it is said that the beloved has *alamma* the heart of the lover, that is, descended upon it. From the same root is *alamma bina*, meaning he came down upon us. From the same usage is his saying:
*"Whenever you visit us in our abodes, you will find firewood piled high and a blazing fire."*

[Section: Sins Are Minor and Major]

Sins are divided into minor and major by the explicit text of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, by the consensus of the early generations (*salaf*), and by reasoning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [al-Nisa': 31].
And the Exalted said: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾ [al-Najm: 32].
In the Sahih, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "The five prayers, and Friday to Friday, and Ramadan to Ramadan, are expiations for what lies between them, if the major sins are avoided."

As for what is related from Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, that he said: "All sins are major sins, and there are no minor sins among them," his intent is not that they are equal in sinfulness, such that the sin of a forbidden gaze equals the sin of unlawful intercourse. Rather, his meaning is that, relative to the greatness of the One who is disobeyed, all of them are major, and yet some of them are greater than others. Even so, the matter in this is verbal and does not reduce to a difference in meaning.

What has come in the Lawgiver's wording is calling these *lamam* and "belittled sins," as in the hadith: "Beware of belittled sins."

It has been said that *al-lamam* mentioned in the verse is one of the major sins, as al-Baghawi and others related. They said: the meaning of the exception is that a person commits a major sin once, then repents from it, or falls into it and then desists, not making it his habit. On this view, the exception of *lamam* from avoidance means that it does not proceed from them, and major sins do not befall them except as *lamam*.

But the majority hold that it is an exception from the major sins, and it is a disjunctive (*munqati'*) exception, meaning: "but they do commit *lamam*."

The disjunctive exception after an affirmative statement is acceptable, though the usual practice is otherwise. It occurs where there is an implicit negation (*tafrigh*), since in the affirmative here there is an explicit sense of negation. The meaning is: "They do not commit or perform the major sins and immoralities," so the exception of *lamam* is appropriate.

Perhaps this is what encouraged Abu Ishaq to say, "All sins are major sins," since the basic principle of exception is connection (*ittisal*), especially when it follows an affirmative.

But the texts and the consensus of the early generations establish that sins are divided into minor and major.

Then the scholars differed on two matters: first, what *lamam* is; second, the major sins, whether they have a number that limits them or a boundary that defines them. Let us mention something related to these two matters.

[Section: The Meaning of Lamam]

As for *lamam*, it has been related from a group of the early generations that it is committing a sin once and then not returning to it, even if it is a major sin. Al-Baghawi said: this is the view of Abu Hurayrah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and a narration of 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas. He said: 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As said: "*Lamam* is what is below polytheism." Al-Suddi said: Abu Salih said: "I was asked about the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿except for minor lapses﴾?" I said: "It is the man who commits a sin and then does not repeat it." I mentioned that to Ibn 'Abbas, and he said: "Verily, a noble angel helped you with it."

The majority hold that *lamam* is less than the major sins, and this is the more authentic of the two narrations from Ibn 'Abbas, as in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, through Tawus from him, who said: "I have seen nothing more similar to *lamam* than what Abu Hurayrah said from the Prophet ﷺ: 'Allah has written for the son of Adam his share of adultery, he will inevitably encounter it. The adultery of the eye is the gaze, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the soul desires and longs, and the private part confirms that or denies it.'" Muslim related it from the hadith of Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, and in it: "The two eyes' adultery is the gaze, the two ears' adultery is listening, the tongue's adultery is speech, the hand's adultery is seizing, and the foot's adultery is stepping."

Al-Kalbi said: "*Lamam* is of two kinds. Every sin for which Allah has not prescribed a legal penalty in this world, nor a punishment in the Hereafter, is what the five prayers expiate, so long as it does not reach the major sins and immoralities. The second kind is a great sin that the Muslim commits once after another, then repents from it."

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "It is what touches the heart," that is, what occurs to it.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "*Lamam* is a gaze without deliberate intent; it is forgiven. If he repeats the gaze, it is no longer *lamam*, and it is a sin." 'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
*"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much, and which of Your servants does not commit lapses?"*

A third group held that *lamam* refers to what they did in the Jahiliyyah before their Islam, for which Allah does not hold them accountable. This is because the polytheists said to the Muslims: "Yesterday you were acting with us," so Allah revealed this verse. This is the view of Zayd ibn Thabit and Zayd ibn Aslam.

The correct view is the majority's, that *lamam* is the minor sins, such as a glance, a flirtatious gesture, a kiss, and the like. This is the view of the majority of the Companions and those after them, and it is the view of Abu Hurayrah, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq, and al-Sha'bi. The view of Abu Hurayrah and Ibn 'Abbas in the other narration, that one commits a major sin once and then does not return to it, does not contradict this. Either *lamam* encompasses both, and is of two kinds as al-Kalbi said, or Abu Hurayrah and Ibn 'Abbas attached to *lamam* the one who committed a major sin only once, without persisting in it, but it happened to him as a lapse in his life. They saw that a sin becomes grave and great only regarding one who repeats it many times. This is among the understanding (*fiqh*) of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and the depth of their knowledge. There is no doubt that Allah forgives His servant once, twice, or thrice, and what is feared is ruin (*'anat*) for one who makes sin his habit and repeats it many times. There are early reports to this effect, and reasoning from reality points to this. It is related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that a thief was brought to him, and he ordered his hand cut off. The man said: "O Commander of the Faithful, by Allah, I have not stolen except this one time." He said: "You lie." When his hand was cut, he said: "Tell me the truth: how many times have you stolen before this?" The man said: "So-and-so many times." He said: "You have spoken the truth. Verily Allah does not hold one accountable for a first sin," or as he said. If the first sin is not *lamam*, it is of its kind and similar to it. The two views from Abu Hurayrah and Ibn 'Abbas are in agreement, not in contradiction, and Allah knows best.

This word carries the meaning of approaching and returning to an act from time to time. It is said: *alamma bi-kadha* when one approaches something without covering it. From this, the kiss and the flirtatious gesture were called *lamam*, because they approach what comes after them. It is also said: "So-and-so does not visit us except occasionally (*limaman*)," meaning from time to time. So the meaning of the word is established in both interpretations the Companions gave of the verse. The meaning of the verse is not "those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except *lamam*, for they do not avoid it," for that would be praise of them for not avoiding *lamam*, which is absurd. Rather, this is an exception from the content and meaning of the sentence. The context of the sentence concerns dividing people into those who do good and those who do evil, and that Allah rewards each according to his deeds. Then He mentioned the doers of good and described them as those who avoid the major sins and immoralities. The implication is that one is not a doer of good who will be rewarded for his goodness and saved from Allah's punishment unless he avoids the major sins and immoralities. Hence the exception of *lamam* is appropriate then, even though it is not included among the major sins, since it falls within the category of sins and immoralities.

[Section: The Disjunctive Exception]

The criterion for a disjunctive exception is that the excepted item belongs to the genus of what is excepted from, even if it is not itself included and its wording does not cover it. Such as the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk, only "Peace"﴾ [Maryam: 62]. Peace is included in speech, which is the genus of idle talk and peace. Likewise His saying: ﴿They taste therein neither coolness nor drink, except boiling water and dark pus﴾ [al-Naba': 24]. Boiling water and dark pus fall within the genus of tasting, which is divided. It is as if it were said in the first: "They hear therein nothing except peace," and in the second: "They taste therein nothing except boiling water and dark pus." He specifically mentioned one of the individual members of the genus explicitly, so that its negation is by explicit mention and specification, not by a general wording that admits the specification of that individual. Likewise His saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of it, except the following of conjecture﴾ [al-Nisa': 157]. Conjecture falls within perception, which is the genus of knowledge and conjecture.

Subtler than this is the disjunctive exception's inclusion of what the speech conveys by necessary implication. Such as the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 22]. The implication of this is that marrying the wives of one's fathers is a cause for punishment, except what has already passed of it before the prohibition, for that is pardoned. Likewise: ﴿And that you join two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. And if what is meant by it is what was in the law of earlier communities, then it is an exception from the ugliness implied by that prohibition and the blame of the one who did it, so it is appropriate to say: "except what has already passed."

Reflect on this, for it is part of the understanding of Arabic.

As for His saying: ﴿They taste therein no death except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56], this exception serves to affirm the permanence of life and the absence of tasting death. It makes the first, general negation equivalent to an explicit text to which no exception at all may be admitted. For if an exception of one individual from its members were admitted, it would have been more fitting to mention it than to turn away to the disjunctive exception. So this exception functions as emphasis and explicit affirmation of preserving the generality. This applies to every disjunctive exception, so reflect on it, for it is among the secrets of Arabic.

Thus the line of poetry: *"And in the open ground there is no one except the stones of the hearths,"* implies that if I had found anyone there, I would have excepted him, and I would not have turned to the stones of the hearths which are not persons.

Close to this is the particle *aw* ("or") in His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones, or even harder in hardness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74], and His saying: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand, or they were more﴾ [al-Saffat: 147]. It is as an explicit statement that what is meant by the first is the literal reality, not hyperbole. For if their hardness did not exceed that of stones, it is at least like stones in hardness, not less. And if their number did not exceed one hundred thousand, it did not fall below it. So the mention of *aw* here is as an explicit affirmation of preserving the figure of one hundred thousand, and that it is not an intended exaggeration. Allah knows best.

[Section: The Major Sins]

As for the major sins, the early generations differed about them in a way that does not amount to contradiction or opposition, and their statements are close to one another.

In the two Sahihs, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The major sins are associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents, killing a soul, and the perjurious oath (*al-yamin al-ghamus*)."

And in both (Sahihs), from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakrah, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Shall I inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" – three times. They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Associating partners with Allah, and disobedience to parents." He had been reclining, then he sat up and said: "Beware, and false speech." He kept repeating it until we said: "I wish he would be silent."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 53, verse 32 (part 2 of 4):

It is related in the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Wa'il, from Amr ibn Surahbil, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, which sin is the greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival (nidd) to Allah while He created you." I said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." I said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour." So Allah the Exalted revealed, confirming the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

And in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what are they?" He said: "Associating partners with Allah, sorcery, killing a soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan, fleeing on the day of the battle-line, and slandering chaste, unwary, believing women."

Shu'bah narrated from Sa'd ibn Ibrahim: I heard Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman narrate from Abdullah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Among the greatest of the major sins is that a man should curse his parents." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how does a man curse his parents?" He said: "A man curses the father of another man, so he curses his father, and curses his mother, so he curses his mother."

And in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Indeed, among the greatest of the major sins is a man's disparaging the honour of his Muslim brother without right."

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The greatest of the major sins are associating partners with Allah, feeling secure from the plan of Allah, despairing of the mercy of Allah, and giving up hope in the comfort of Allah."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man asked Ibn Abbas about the major sins, "Are they seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seven hundred. However, there is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence." And he said: "Everything with which Allah is disobeyed is a major sin. Whoever commits any of them should seek forgiveness from Allah, for Allah does not cause to dwell eternally in the Fire of the Ummah anyone except one who has renounced Islam, or one who denies an obligation, or one who denies the divine decree (qadar)."

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Whatever Allah has forbidden in Surat al-Nisa' from its beginning up to His saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [al-Nisa': 31], is a major sin.

Ali ibn Abi Talhah said: They are every sin which Allah has concluded with a Fire, or wrath, or a curse, or a punishment.

Al-Dahhak said: They are what Allah has threatened a prescribed penalty for in this world, or a punishment in the Hereafter.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: They are what Allah has named in the Qur'an as great (kabir) or mighty ('azim), such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, it was a great sin (hububan kabiran)﴾ [al-Nisa': 2]; ﴿Indeed, their killing was a great offence (khit'an kabiran)﴾ [al-Isra': 31]; ﴿Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]; ﴿Indeed, your plotting is tremendous﴾ [Yusuf: 28]; ﴿Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander﴾ [al-Nur: 16]; ﴿Indeed, that was in the sight of Allah tremendous﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53].

Sufyan al-Thawri said: The major sins are those involving wrongs between you and the servants, and the minor sins are those between you and Allah, because Allah is Generous and pardons. He cited the hadith of Yazid ibn Harun, from Humayd al-Tawil, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A caller will call from the direction of the bottom of the Throne on the Day of Resurrection: O community of Muhammad, indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has pardoned all of you, the believing men and believing women, so forgive one another's wrongs among yourselves, and enter Paradise by My mercy."

I say: Sufyan's meaning is that the sins between the servant and Allah are easier in matter than the wrongs done to the servants, for they are removed by seeking forgiveness, pardon, intercession and other means. As for the wrongs done to the servants, they must be settled.

In al-Mu'jam by al-Tabarani: Wrongdoing before Allah on the Day of Resurrection consists of three registers:
A register which Allah will not forgive in any part, and it is associating partners with Allah. Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. A register which Allah will not leave in any part, and it is the wrongs of the servants against one another. And a register which Allah will not regard at all, and it is a servant's wronging of himself between himself and Allah.

It is known that this register includes both major and minor sins, but its entitled party is the most generous of the generous, and what He pardons of His right and gives away is many times more than what He exacts. Thus its matter is easier than the register which He does not leave in any part, because of His justice and the delivery of every right to its owner.

Malik ibn Mighwal said: The major sins are the sins of the people of innovation (bid'ah), and the misdeeds are the sins of the people of the Sunnah.

I say: He means that innovation is among the major sins, and that it is greater than the major sins of the people of the Sunnah; so the major sins of the people of the Sunnah are minor in comparison with innovations. This is the meaning of the saying of some of the early generations: "Innovation is more beloved to Iblis than disobedience, because one does not repent from innovation, whereas one repents from disobedience."

It has been said: The major sins are sins committed deliberately, and the misdeeds are errors, forgetfulness, what one is compelled to, and the whisperings of the soul, which are lifted from this Ummah.

I say: This is among the weakest of the statements in both inclusion and exclusion, for error, forgetfulness and compulsion do not fall under the category of acts of disobedience so as to be one of its two divisions. Deliberate acts are of two kinds: a kind of major sins and a kind of minor sins. Perhaps the proponent of this view holds that all sins are major sins, and that the minor sins are those which Allah has pardoned for this Ummah and which do not fall under the obligation. This is not correct, for major and minor sins are two kinds under the genus of disobedience, and it is impossible for a kind to exist without its genus.

It has been said: The major sins are the sins of those who make the forbidden lawful, like the sin of Iblis, and the minor sins are the sins of those who seek forgiveness, like the sin of Adam.

I say: As for the one who makes the forbidden lawful, his sin lies between disbelief and interpretation: if he knows the prohibition, he is a disbeliever; and if he does not know it, he is either one who interprets or one who follows another's opinion. As for the one who seeks forgiveness, his complete seeking of forgiveness erases his major and minor sins, so there is no major sin with seeking forgiveness.

This distinction is also weak, unless its proponent means that the sin committed by one who makes it lawful carries a greater punishment than what is committed by one who acknowledges its prohibition, regrets the sin, and seeks forgiveness for it; and this is correct.

Al-Suddi said: The major sins are what Allah has forbidden of the great sins, and the misdeeds are their preliminaries and their consequences, which both the righteous and the wicked share, such as a glance, a touch, a kiss and the like. He cited the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The two eyes commit adultery, the two feet commit adultery, and the private part either confirms all of that or denies it."

It has been said: The major sins are what the servants regard as small, and the minor sins are what they regard as great, so they fear committing them. The proponents of this view cited what al-Bukhari related in his Sahih from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "Indeed you do deeds which in your eyes are finer than hair; in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) we counted them among the destructive sins."

I say: As for al-Suddi's statement, "The major sins are what Allah has forbidden of the great sins," it is an explanation of the thing by itself, for the great sins are the major sins. What he means is that what is forbidden is of two kinds. One is what contains corruption in itself, and the very doing of it is the source of corruption; this is a major sin, such as killing a soul, theft, slander and fornication. The second is what is among the preliminaries and beginnings of those, such as looking, touching, conversation and kissing, which are the preliminaries to fornication; this is among the minor sins. So the minor sins are of the genus of preliminaries, and the major sins are of the genus of ends and goals.

As for the one who said: "What the servants regard as small is major, and what they regard as great is minor," if he means that the distinction returns to their magnifying and minimising, then it is false, for a servant regards a glance as small and regards fornication as great.

But if he means that their regarding a sin as small makes it great in the sight of Allah, and their regarding it as great makes it small in the sight of Allah, then this is correct, for the more a servant's sins are small in his own eyes, the greater they are in the sight of Allah, and the more they are great in his eyes, the smaller they are in the sight of Allah. The hadith only indicates this meaning, for the Companions, because of the lofty rank they held before Allah and their perfection, used to count those deeds as destructive; and those after them, because of the deficiency of their rank compared with theirs and the disparity between them, found those deeds finer than hair in their eyes.

If you wish to understand this, look: was there among the Companions anyone who, when he heard the text of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), opposed it with his analogy, his taste, his feeling, his intellect or his policy? And was there ever any one of them who put intellect, analogy, taste, policy or the imitation of an imitator before the text of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Allah honoured their eyes and preserved them from looking at the face of one whose condition was thus, or who lived in their time. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) judged, by the sword, one who put his judgment before the text of the Messenger, and said: "This is my ruling concerning him." Alas, by Allah! How would he be if he saw what we have seen, and witnessed what we have been afflicted with, of preferring the opinion of this one and that one over the saying of the Infallible (ﷺ), and enmity toward whoever discards their opinions and prefers the saying of the Infallible over them! Allah is the One sought for help, and He is the One promised, and to Him is the return.

It has been said: The major sins are associating partners with Allah and what leads to it, and the minor sins are what is other than shirk from the sins of the people of tawhid.

The proponents of this view cited the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48].

They also cited the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), related from his Lord, blessed and exalted: "O son of Adam, if you come to Me with earth-full of sins, then meet Me not associating anything with Me, I will come to you with its equivalent in forgiveness."

They also cited the hadith which is related both as marfu' and mawquf: "Wrongdoing is three registers: a register which Allah will not forgive in any part, and it is shirk; a register which Allah will not leave in any part, and it is the wronging of servants one another; and a register which Allah does not regard at all, and it is a servant's wronging of himself between himself and his Lord."

This is the sum of what the proponents of this view cited, and there is no proof for them in any of it.

As for the verse, its ultimate import is to distinguish between shirk and other than it, for shirk is not forgiven except by repenting from it, whereas what is less than shirk is left to the will of Allah. This indicates that acts of disobedience other than shirk are so, and this is true. If the proponents of this view mean this, there is no dispute over it; but if they mean that everything other than shirk is in itself a minor sin, then this is false.

If it is said: If shirk and other than it are both things which repentance can erase, what is the basis of the distinction between shirk and what is less than it? Are they both concerning the one who repents, or the one who does not repent, or is one of them concerning the one who repents and the other concerning someone else? And what is the difference between this verse and His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed, Allah forgives all sins; indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]?

The answer is that each of the two verses is for a particular group. The verse of al-Nisa', ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], is for those who do not repent, in both categories.

The proof of this is that He made a distinction between shirk and other than it in forgiveness, and it is known necessarily from the religion of Islam that shirk is forgiven by repentance, for otherwise the Islam of a disbeliever would never be valid.

Also, He restricted the forgiveness of what is less than shirk to whomever He wills, whereas the forgiveness of sins for the repentant is general with no restriction in it. So He restricted and qualified, and this indicates that it is the ruling for one who does not repent.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 53, verse 32 (part 3 of 4):

As for the verse of az-Zumar, ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ [az-Zumar: 53], it refers to the one who repents, because it is unrestricted and general. It does not single out anyone, nor does it limit itself to a particular sin. It is known by necessity that disbelief is not forgiven, and many sins are not forgiven either. Therefore it is known that this unrestricted and general statement applies to the one who repents: whoever repents from any sin whatsoever is forgiven.

As for the other hadith, "If you were to meet Me with earth's worth of sins, then meet Me without associating anything with Me, I would bring you forgiveness equal to it," it does not indicate that everything other than shirk is minor sins. Rather, it indicates that whoever does not associate anything with Allah, his sins are forgiven, whatever they may be. However, it is necessary to recognise the connection between the faith of the hearts and the deeds of the limbs, and their attachment to one another; otherwise the intent of the Messenger ﷺ will not be understood, and confusion and muddle will arise.

Know that this general negation of shirk, that one should associate nothing whatsoever with Allah, never proceeds from one who persists in disobedience. The one addicted to a major sin, or persisting in a minor sin, cannot have pure tawhid such that he does not associate anything with Allah. This is among the greatest impossibilities. Do not heed a disputant who has no share of the deeds of the heart, whose heart is like a stone or harder, who says: "What prevents it? What is the basis of the impossibility?"

Even if that were assumed to occur, it would not entail something impossible in itself!

So leave that heart, which is afflicted by its argumentation and ignorance. Know that persisting in disobedience necessarily brings about, in the heart, fear of other than Allah, hope in other than Allah, love of other than Allah, humiliation before other than Allah, and reliance upon other than Allah, to the degree that one becomes immersed in the seas of shirk. The judge in this is what a person knows of himself, if he has intellect, for the humiliation of disobedience must settle in the heart, producing fear of other than Allah, and that is shirk; and it produces love for other than Allah, and seeking help from others in the means that lead to one's aim, so that his action is neither by Allah nor for Allah. This is the reality of shirk.

Yes, it may be accompanied by the tawhid of Abu Jahl and the idol-worshippers, which is tawhid of Lordship, namely acknowledging that there is no creator except Allah. Had this tawhid alone sufficed, it would have saved the idol-worshippers. The matter lies in the tawhid of Divinity (uluhiyyah), which is the distinguishing mark between the polytheists and the monotheists.

The point is that one who does not associate anything with Allah cannot possibly meet Allah with earth's worth of sins, persisting in them and not repenting from them, while his tawhid is complete, which is the utmost of love, submission, humiliation, fear and hope toward the Lord, exalted is He.

As for the hadith of the registers, it only means that the right of the Lord, exalted is He, does not burden Him to forgive and remit it, nor does He give it the attention and care that He gives to the rights of His servants. Its meaning is not that He never holds someone accountable for it, nor that it is all minor sins. Rather, its meaning is that in the rights of Allah there occurs a degree of leniency, tolerance, remission and pardon that does not occur similarly in the rights of human beings.

Thus it is clear that they have no proof in anything they have cited. And Allah knows best.

Another group said: minor sins are those that fall below the two limits (ḥaddayn), and major sins are those to which one of the two limits is attached.

By the two limits they mean the punishment of this world and the Hereafter. So every sin that carries a prescribed, defined punishment in this world, such as fornication, drinking wine, theft and slander, or that carries a threat in the Hereafter, such as consuming the property of orphans, drinking from vessels of silver and gold, a person killing himself, betraying his trust, and the like, is among the major sins. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, spoke truly when he said: "It is nearer to seven hundred than to seven."

[Chapter: The states in which a major sin becomes minor and vice versa]

Here is a matter that should be carefully noticed: a major sin may be accompanied, by modesty, fear and magnifying it, by things that reduce it to the level of minor sins; and a minor sin may be accompanied, by little modesty, indifference, abandoning fear, and treating it lightly, by things that raise it to the level of major sins, indeed place it at the highest of their ranks.

This matter returns to what subsists in the heart, which is a quantity beyond the mere act, and a person knows this from himself and from others.

Also, the one who loves, and the one who has great benevolence, is pardoned what is not pardoned to others, and is tolerated in what others are not tolerated.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his soul, say: Look at Musa, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him: he threw down the tablets upon which was the speech of Allah which He had written with His own hand, and broke them; he dragged by the beard a prophet like himself, Harun; he slapped the eye of the Angel of Death until he gouged it out; and he rebuked his Lord on the night of the Isra' concerning Muhammad ﷺ and preferred him above himself. Yet his Lord, exalted is He, bore all of that for him, loved him, honoured him, and treated him with tenderness, because he had stood for Allah in those great stations against the greatest enemy of His, had proclaimed His command, and had dealt with the two nations, the Copts and the Children of Israel, with the utmost struggle; so these matters were like a hair in the sea.

Now look at Yunus ibn Matta, who did not have these stations that Musa had: he became angry with his Lord once, so He seized him and imprisoned him in the belly of the fish, and He did not bear for him what He bore for Musa. There is a difference between one who commits a single sin and has no good deeds or virtues to intercede for him, and one who commits a sin and whose virtues come with every intercessor, as it is said:

"When the beloved commits a single sin, his virtues come with a thousand intercessors."

Deeds intercede for their doer with Allah, and remind Him of him when he falls into hardships. The Exalted said concerning Dhu al-Nun: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify [Allah], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [as-Saffat: 143-144].

As for Pharaoh, since he had no precedent of good to intercede for him, he said: ﴿I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel have believed﴾ [Yunus: 90], and Jibril said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before, and were among the corrupters﴾ [Yunus: 91].

In the Musnad, from him ﷺ, that he said: "Indeed, what you mention of the majesty of Allah, of tasbih, takbir and tahmid, circles around the Throne, having a hum like the hum of bees, reminding of their companion. Does not one of you love to have something that reminds of him?" For this reason, whoever's good deeds outweigh his evil deeds succeeds and is not punished, and his evil deeds are forgiven for the sake of his good deeds. For this reason, the people of tawhid are forgiven what the people of shirk are not forgiven, because the servant has performed what Allah loves, which required that He forgive him and overlook from him what He does not overlook from the polytheist. And just as the servant's tawhid is greater, Allah's forgiveness of him is more complete. Whoever meets Him without associating anything with Him whatsoever, He forgives him all his sins, whatever they may be, and does not punish him for them.

We do not say that none of the people of tawhid enters the Fire; rather, many of them enter it because of their sins, and are punished according to the measure of their crime, then they are brought out of it. There is no contradiction between the two matters for one who has comprehensive knowledge of what we have set forth.

Here we add further clarification of the greatness of this station, given how great the need for it is: know that the rays of "There is no god but Allah" disperse, from the haze and clouds of sins, according to the strength and weakness of that ray. It has a light, and the people of it differ in that light, in strength and weakness, in a way that none can count except Allah, exalted is He.

Among people is one in whose heart the light of this word is like the sun.
And among them is one in whose heart its light is like a brilliant star.
And among them is one in whose heart its light is like a great torch.
Another is like a shining lamp, and another like a weak lamp.

For this reason, on the Day of Resurrection the lights will appear in their right hands and before them, to this measure, according to what is in their hearts of the light of this word, in knowledge and action, in recognition and state.

Whenever the light of this word grows great and intense, it burns up doubts and desires according to its strength and intensity, until it may reach a state in which it encounters no doubt, no desire, and no sin without burning it up. This is the state of the one truthful in his tawhid, who has not associated anything with Allah. Whatever sin, desire or doubt draws near to this light, it burns it. The sky of his faith has been guarded with stars against every thief of his good deeds, so the thief takes from it only through heedlessness and negligence, which are unavoidable for humankind. When he awakens and knows what was stolen from him, he rescues it from its thief, or gains its equivalent many times over through his effort. He is always like this with the thieves of jinn and humankind, unlike one who opens his treasury to them and turns his back on the door.

Tawhid is not merely the servant's acknowledgment that there is no creator except Allah, and that Allah is the Lord and Owner of everything, as the idol-worshippers acknowledged this while they were polytheists. Rather, tawhid includes love of Allah, submission to Him, humiliation before Him, complete compliance with His obedience, sincerity of worship to Him, desiring His noble countenance with all words and deeds, in giving and withholding, in love and hatred, what stands between its possessor and the causes that call to acts of disobedience and persistence in them. Whoever knows this understands the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah has forbidden the Fire to one who says: There is no god but Allah, seeking by that the face of Allah," and his saying: "No one who says 'There is no god but Allah' will enter the Fire," and what comes of this kind of hadith, which has puzzled many people, so that some thought it abrogated, some thought it was said before the commands and prohibitions were revealed and the Sharia was established, some interpreted it as referring to the fire of the polytheists and disbelievers, some interpreted "entering" as "remaining forever," and other such far-fetched interpretations.

The Lawgiver, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, did not make this achieved merely by the utterance of the tongue alone, for that contradicts what is known by necessity from the religion of Islam, since the hypocrites say it with their tongues while they are beneath those who deny it, in the lowest level of the Fire. Therefore there must be both the speech of the heart and the speech of the tongue. The speech of the heart includes knowledge of it, belief in it, and knowledge of the reality of what it contains, of negation and affirmation, and knowledge of the reality of the divinity negated from other than Allah, specific to Him, whose establishment for another is impossible. The subsistence of this meaning in the heart, in knowledge, recognition, certainty and state, is what necessitates forbidding its utterer to the Fire. Every statement for which the Lawgiver has prescribed reward is the complete statement, such as his saying ﷺ: "Whoever says in a day: Glory be to Allah and praise Him, a hundred times, his sins are removed from him, or his sins are forgiven, even if they were like the foam of the sea."

This is not conditioned merely on the utterance of the tongue.

Yes, whoever says it with his tongue, heedless of its meaning, turning away from reflecting upon it, his heart not in accord with his tongue, nor recognising its worth and reality, yet hoping for its reward, its effect on his sins is reduced according to what is in his heart. Deeds do not differ in their forms or numbers; they differ only according to what is in the hearts. Two acts may have the same form, yet between them in rank there is a difference like that between heaven and earth. Two men may stand in the same row, yet between their prayers there is a difference like that between heaven and earth.

Consider the hadith of the card (bitaqah) that is placed on one pan of the scale, opposite which are ninety-nine registers, each register extending as far as the eye can see; the card outweighs them, and the registers are light, so he is not punished.

It is known that every monotheist has a card like this, and many of them enter the Fire because of their sins. But the secret that made that man's card heavy, and made the registers light for his sake, was not present in the others who possess cards; so his card alone was singled out for weight and gravity.

And when you wish to increase the clarity of this meaning, consider the mention of one whose heart is filled with love for You, and the mention of one who turns away from You, heedless and unmindful, preoccupied with other than You, whose heart's motives have been drawn toward love of other than You and preferring it over You. Would the mention of these two be the same? Or would your two sons, who stand in this same position, or your two servants, or your two wives, be equal in your sight?

Reflect on what arose in the heart of the man who had killed one hundred people: realities of faith that did not preoccupy him, at the moment of death, from setting out for the village, and which moved him, in that state, to begin to struggle with his chest and to undergo the agonies of death. This is a different matter and a different faith, and it is no wonder that he was granted admission to the righteous village and was counted among its people.

Close to this is what arose in the heart of the prostitute who saw that dog, its thirst having grown intense so that it was eating the moist earth. At that moment there arose in her heart, despite lacking the means, lacking a helper, and lacking anyone whom she might show off to by her deed, what moved her to risk herself by descending into the well, filling her leather sock with water, and paying no heed to the exposure of herself to destruction. She carried the sock in her mouth while it was full, until she was able to climb out of the well. Then she humbled herself before this creature, which people customarily strike, and held the sock for it with her hand until it drank, without hoping from it for any reward or gratitude. The lights of this measure of monotheism burned away what had preceded it of her prostitution, and so she was forgiven.

Thus it is with deeds and doers in the sight of God. The heedless one is in a state of neglect regarding this chemical elixir, which, if a mere particle's weight of it is placed upon heaps of the copper of deeds, turns them into gold. And God is the One sought for help.

**Section**

Ahmad [ibn Hanbal] was asked about a man who does a good deed and gives half of its reward to his father or to his mother. He said: "I hope [it reaches them]."

He also said: "Everything good reaches the dead, because of what has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'Among the acts of righteousness after the righteous acts is that you pray for them along with your prayer, fast for them along with your fast, and give charity on their behalf along with your charity.'" End of quotation.

It is not required to name the person to whom the reward is gifted; intention suffices. He stated this in the narration of his son Abdullah: "There is no harm in performing Hajj on behalf of a man without naming him."

**[Section: The arrival of the reward of charity]**

As for the arrival of the reward of charity, (it is in the two Sahihs [Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim]) from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother died suddenly without making a bequest, and I think that if she had been able to speak, she would have given charity. Will she have a reward if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." (1)

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Sa'd ibn Ubadah's mother died while he was absent from her. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother has died while I was absent from her. Will it benefit her if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then I call you to witness that my garden, al-Mikhraf, is a charity on her behalf." (2)

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah: a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "My father died and left wealth, and he did not make a bequest. Will it expiate for him if I give charity on his behalf?" He said: "Yes."

In the Sunan and in Musnad Ahmad, from Sa'd ibn Ubadah, that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, Sa'd's mother has died; which charity is best?" He said: "Water." So he dug a well and said: "This is for the mother of Sa'd."

From Abdullah ibn Amr: al-As ibn Wa'il vowed in the pre-Islamic period to sacrifice one hundred camels, and Hisham ibn al-As sacrificed fifty-five. Amr asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about that, and he said: "As for your father, had he affirmed the Oneness [of Allah], then fasting on his behalf and giving charity on his behalf would have benefited him." Related by Imam Ahmad.

**[Section: The arrival of the reward of fasting]**

As for the arrival of the reward of fasting, (it is in the two Sahihs) from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies owing fasts, his guardian shall fast on his behalf." (1)

(And in the two Sahihs) also from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother died and owed a month of fasting. Shall I make it up on her behalf?" He said: "If your mother had a debt, would you have paid it?" He said: "Yes." (2) He said: "The debt owed to Allah is more deserving of being paid." (3)

In another narration: A woman came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother died and owed fasts for a vow. Shall I fast on her behalf?" He said: "Do you see, if your mother had a debt and you paid it, would that have discharged it for her?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then fast on behalf of your mother." This wording is that of al-Bukhari alone, as a suspended (mu'allaq) narration. (4)

From Bureydah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "While I was sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a woman came to him and said: 'I gave my mother a slave-girl as charity, and she has died.' He said: 'Your reward is due, and the inheritance has returned it to you.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, she owed a month of fasting; shall I fast on her behalf?' He said: 'Fast on her behalf.' She said: 'She never performed Hajj; shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?' He said: 'Perform Hajj on her behalf.'" Related by Muslim. In another wording: "two months of fasting." (5)

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a woman boarded a ship and vowed that if Allah saved her, she would fast for a month. Allah saved her, but she did not fast until she died. Then her daughter or her sister came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he commanded her to fast on her behalf. Related by the authors of the Sunan and by Imam Ahmad.

Likewise, it has been related from him (ﷺ) that the reward of a substitute for fasting, which is feeding the poor, reaches the dead.

In the Sunan, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies owing a month of fasting, let him feed a poor person on his behalf for each day." Related by al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah. Al-Tirmidhi said: "We do not know it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) narration except through this route, and the sound report from Ibn Umar is his own statement, mawquf (halted at the companion)." (1)

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "If a man falls ill during Ramadan and does not fast, food is given on his behalf and there is no makeup obligation. If he owed a vow, his guardian makes it up on his behalf." (2) (3)

**[Section: The arrival of the reward of Hajj]**

As for the arrival of the reward of Hajj, in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a woman from Juhaynah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My mother vowed to perform Hajj but died without performing it. Shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?" He said: "Perform Hajj on her behalf. Do you see, if your mother had a debt, would you have paid it? Pay what is owed to Allah, for Allah is more deserving of being paid." (4)

The narration of Bureydah has already been mentioned, in which [the woman said]: "My mother did not perform Hajj; shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?" He said: "Perform Hajj on her behalf."

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The woman of Sinan ibn Salamah al-Juhani was commanded to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that her mother had died without performing Hajj: "Is it sufficient that she perform Hajj on her behalf?" He said: "Yes. If your mother had a debt and you paid it on her behalf, would that not have sufficed for her? So let her perform Hajj on behalf of her mother." Related by al-Nasa'i. (5)

It has also been related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a woman asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about her father who died without performing Hajj. He said: "Perform Hajj on behalf of your father."

It has also been related from him, who said: A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, my father died without performing Hajj; shall I perform Hajj on his behalf?" He said: "Do you see, if your father had a debt, would you have paid it?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then the debt owed to Allah is more deserving."

The Muslims have agreed that the payment of a debt discharges it from the debtor's liability, even if it is paid by a stranger or from outside his estate. The narration of Abu Qatadah also indicates this, when he guaranteed two dinars on behalf of the deceased, and when he paid them the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Now his skin has cooled." (6)

They have also agreed that if a living person has a right against a deceased person, and the living person forgives it, that benefits the deceased and frees him from it, just as it discharges the liability of a living debtor.

So if it is discharged from the liability of a living debtor by textual evidence and consensus, even when it is possible for the creditor to collect it personally, and even if he does not consent but refuses it, then its discharge from the liability of a deceased person by pardon, when he cannot pay it, is more fitting and more deserving. And if the deceased benefits from pardon and remission, then likewise he benefits from a gift and an offering. There is no difference between them. For the reward of an act is the right of the one who offers it and gives it; so if he makes it for the deceased, it passes to him, just as the rights owed by the deceased, whether debt or otherwise, are purely the right of the living; so if he forgives them, the forgiveness reaches the deceased and he is released from liability. Both are rights of the living. So what text, analogy (qiyas), or rule of the Sharia requires the arrival of one of them while preventing the arrival of the other?

These texts are consistent in establishing that the rewards of deeds reach the dead when the living perform them on their behalf. This is pure analogy: the reward is the right of the one who performs the act, so if he gives it to his Muslim brother, he is not prevented from doing so, just as he is not prevented from giving away his property during his life or forgiving a debt after his death.

The Prophet (ﷺ) has indicated the arrival of the reward of fasting, which is merely abstention and an intention established in the heart that no one knows of but Allah, and which is not an act of the limbs. Then the arrival of the reward of recitation, which is an act of the tongue heard by the ear and seen by the eye, is all the more fitting. This is further clarified by the fact that fasting is pure intention and restraining oneself from the things that break the fast; and Allah has caused its reward to reach the dead. How much more so recitation, which is an act and an intention, and indeed does not require intention. So the arrival of the reward of fasting to the dead indicates the arrival of all other deeds.

Acts of worship are of two kinds: financial and physical. The Lawgiver has indicated, by the arrival of the reward of charity, the arrival of the reward of all other financial acts of worship, and by the arrival of the reward of fasting, the arrival of all other physical acts of worship; and he informed that the reward of Hajj, which combines the financial and the physical, arrives. So the three categories are established by textual evidence and reasoned inference. And success is from Allah.

**[The arguments of those who deny arrival]**

Those who deny the arrival [of rewards] said: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ (1). He also said: ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾ (2). And He said: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾ (3). It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When a servant dies, his deeds end, except for three: an ongoing charity, a righteous child who prays for him, or knowledge from which people benefit after him." (4) So he informed that a person benefits only from what he was the cause of during his life; and what he was not the cause of has ended for him.

Also, the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned earlier, which is his saying: "Among what reaches a dead person from his deeds and good works after his death is knowledge that he spread." This hadith indicates that he benefits only from what he himself caused.

Likewise the hadith of Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Seven things whose reward continues to flow to the servant while he is in his grave after his death: one who taught knowledge, or dug a canal, or dug a well, or planted a palm tree, or built a mosque, or left a copy of the Qur'an as an inheritance, or left a righteous child who asks forgiveness for him after his death." This indicates that anything beyond these does not yield him reward; otherwise the enumeration would have no meaning.

They said: Offering is a transfer (hawalah), and a transfer is only valid for a binding right, while deeds do not necessitate reward; it is merely Allah's grace and kindness. How then can a servant transfer to another what is merely grace, which is not obligatory upon Allah? Rather, if He wills He gives it, and if He does not will, He does not give it. This is like the transfer of a poor man to someone he hopes will give him charity. Such a thing is not valid to offer or to give as a gift, like a gift hoped for from a king which is not certain to be received.

They said: Also, preferring others with the means of reward is disliked, and that is preferring others with acts of devotion. How much more so preferring others with the reward itself, which is the goal? If preferring others with the means is disliked, then the goal is more fitting [to be disliked]. Likewise Imam Ahmad disliked delaying from the first row and giving it up to a grave, because of the desire to avoid the cause of reward.

Ahmad said in the narration of Hanbal, when he was asked about a man who delays from the first row and lets his father take his place there: "I do not like it. He can be dutiful to his father without this."

They said: Also, if it were permissible to offer [reward] to the dead, it would be permissible to transfer the reward and offer it to the living. Also, if that were permissible, then a half of the reward, or a quarter of it, or a qirat of it, would be permissible for him.

Also, if that were permissible, it would be permissible to offer it after performing the act for oneself. And you have said that one must intend, at the time of the act, to offer it to the dead, otherwise it does not reach him. So if it is permissible for him to transfer the reward, what difference is there between intending before the act or after it?

Also, if offering were permissible, it would be permissible to offer the reward of obligatory acts by the living, just as it is permissible to offer the reward of the voluntary acts one performs.

They said: Obligations are a test and a trial that do not accept substitution, for their purpose is the very person of the responsible one who acts, is commanded and forbidden. So the responsible one under test is not replaced by another, nor does another stand in for him in that, since the purpose is his own obedience and his own servitude. If he could benefit from another's offering without any act on his part, the Most Generous of the generous would be more worthy of that. And He, glorified be He, has decreed that a person benefits only from seven things, and this is His way with His creation and His decree, just as it is His way with His command and His law. A sick man is not represented by another in drinking medicine, and a hungry, thirsty, or naked person is not represented by another in eating, drinking, or clothing. They said: If the act of another benefited him, then his repentance would benefit him in that way.

They said: For this reason, Allah does not accept the Islam of one person on behalf of another, nor his ritual purity on behalf of another's. So if the very foundation of acts of worship cannot have its reward offered, how much less its branches?

[The one who holds this view] said: As for supplication, it is a request and an expression of desire to Allah that He bestow His grace upon the dead, pardon him, and forgive him; and this is the offering of the reward of the living's act to him.

**[The position of those who restrict arrival to acts in which substitution is admissible]**

Those who restrict the arrival [of reward] to acts of worship that admit substitution, such as charity and Hajj, said: Acts of worship are of two kinds:

One kind does not admit substitution at all, such as Islam, prayer, recitation of the Qur'an, and fasting. The reward of this kind belongs exclusively to its doer and is not transferred or passed on from him, just as during his life no one performs it on behalf of another, and no one stands in for its doer.

Another kind admits substitution, such as returning deposits, paying debts, giving out charity, and Hajj. The reward of this reaches the dead, because it admits substitution, and a servant performs it on behalf of another during his life; so after his death it is all the more so, and in every way.

They said: As for the hadith, "Whoever dies owing fasts, his guardian shall fast on his behalf," its answer is in several ways:

First: What Malik said in his Muwatta': "No one fasts on behalf of anyone else." He said: "This is a matter agreed upon among us, with no disagreement about it."

Second: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is the one who related the hadith about fasting on behalf of the dead, yet al-Nasa'i related from him: (We were informed by) Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la, who said: Yazid ibn Zurai' told us, who said: Hajjaj al-Ahwal told us, who said: Ayyub ibn Musa told us, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "No one prays on behalf of anyone else."

Third: It is a hadith whose chain is disputed, as the author of al-Mufhim in his commentary on Muslim said.

Fourth: It contradicts the text of the Qur'an, as mentioned above, in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾.

Fifth: It contradicts what al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No one prays on behalf of anyone else, and no one fasts on behalf of anyone else; but one feeds on his behalf a mudd of wheat for each day."

Sixth: It contradicts the hadith of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever dies owing the fasts of Ramadan, let food be given on his behalf."

Seventh: It contradicts clear analogy regarding prayer, Islam, and repentance, for no one performs them on behalf of another.

Al-Shafi'i said, in what he said about the report of Ibn Abbas, without naming Ibn Abbas: "What was the vow of the mother of Sa'd? It is possible that it was a vow of Hajj, or 'umrah, or charity, and he commanded him to fulfil it on her behalf. As for one who vows prayer or fasting and then dies, he makes expiation for it in the case of fasting, but fasting is not performed on his behalf, nor is prayer performed on his behalf, nor is expiation made for it in the case of prayer." Then he said: "If it is said: Has it been related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he commanded someone to fast on behalf of another?" It is answered: "Yes, Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, related it from the Prophet (ﷺ)." If it is said: "Then why do you not act upon it?" It is answered: The hadith of al-Zuhri from Ubayd Allah from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), [mentions] a vow and does not name it, despite al-Zuhri's memorization and Ubayd Allah's long companionship with Ibn Abbas. When another related it from a man, from Ibn Abbas, with wording different from the hadith of Ubayd Allah, it is more likely that it is not preserved." If it is said: "Then identify the man who brought this hadith, who erred regarding Ibn Abbas." It is answered: "Yes: the companions of Ibn Abbas related from Ibn Abbas that he said to Ibn al-Zubayr: 'Al-Zubayr released himself from the Hajj tamattu',' and this was related from Ibn Abbas as [referring to] the enjoyment of women; and this is a gross error."

This is the answer regarding the act of fasting. As for the act of Hajj, only the reward of the expenditure reaches the dead; and as for the acts of the rites, they are like the acts of prayer, which only their doer performs.

**[The reply of the proponents of arrival]**

The proponents of arrival said: Nothing in what you have mentioned contradicts the evidence of the Book and the Sunnah, the consensus of the early community, and the requirements of the rules of the Sharia. We answer everything you have mentioned with justice and fairness.

As for the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾:

People have differed regarding the meaning of the verse. One group said: the word "man" here means the disbeliever; as for the believer, he has what he strove for and what was strived for on his behalf, by the evidence we have mentioned. They said: The most that this restriction involves is that it is permissible, since evidence indicates it.

This answer is very weak. A general term like this is not meant to refer to the disbeliever alone; rather it includes both the Muslim and the disbeliever, and it is like the general term before it, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ (1).

The whole context, from beginning to end, is virtually explicit in intending the general sense, because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And that his striving will be seen, then he will be recompensed with the fullest recompense﴾ (2). This certainly encompasses both good and evil, and it includes the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ (3).

And like His saying in the divine hadith: "O My servants, these are only your deeds, which I count for you and then repay you in full. So whoever finds good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds other than that, let him blame no one but himself." And it is like His saying the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet it﴾ (4).

*Notes on footnote markers in the source:* (1) Sahih al-Bukhari; (2) Sahih al-Bukhari; (3) Sahih al-Bukhari; (4) ... *(Numbers as in source, where they appear.)*

Do not be deceived by the statement of many exegetes (mufassirun) about the word "al-insan" (the human being) in the Qur'an, that "the human being here is Abu Jahl," "the human being here is 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt," or "the human being here is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira." The Qur'an is far above that. Rather, al-insan is the human being as such, without being restricted to any particular individual, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾, and ﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord﴾, and ﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious﴾, and ﴿Indeed, mankind transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾, and ﴿Indeed, mankind is ever a wrongdoer, a disbeliever﴾, and ﴿And mankind bore it; indeed, he was a wrongdoer and ignorant﴾.

This is the condition of the human being in terms of his essence and self. His departure from these qualities is by the bounty of his Lord, by His enabling him, and by His favor upon him, not from himself. He has from himself nothing but these qualities, and whatever blessing he has is from Allah alone. It is He who made faith beloved to His servant and beautified it in his heart, and made disbelief, transgression and disobedience hateful to him. It is He who wrote faith in his heart, and it is He who keeps His prophets, messengers and friends firm in His religion, and it is He who turns evil and indecency away from them.

The Prophet ﷺ used to hear a rajaz (a poetic meter) recited before him:
"By Allah, had it not been for Allah, we would not have been guided, nor would we have given charity, nor would we have prayed."

And Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾.
And Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And they will not remember unless Allah wills﴾.
And: ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾. So He is the Lord of all the worlds, with a comprehensive lordship over everything in the world, of essences, actions and states.

A group said: the verse is a report about the law of those before us, and our law has shown that for him is what he strove for and what was strived for him. This too is weaker than the first, or of its kind, for Allah, glorified is He, reported it as a confirming report by which He argues, not a report that nullifies it. Hence He said: ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scrolls of Moses?﴾ If this were false in this law, He would not have reported it as a confirmed and argued-for matter.

Another group said: the lam means "upon" (ʿala), i.e., "and there is not upon the human being except what he strove for." This is more false than the two previous views, for it turns the subject of the speech into its opposite meaning, and language does not permit this. As for the like of ﴿and for them is the curse﴾, it is in its own usage, meaning their share and portion. As for the claim that the Arabs know in their dialects that "li dirham" means "ʿalayya dirham," no.

Another group said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its estimate being: ﴿and that there is not for the human being except what he strove for﴾, or "what was strived for him." This too is of the first type, for it omits what the context does not indicate at all, and it speaks about Allah and His Book without knowledge.

Another group said: the verse is abrogated (naskh, abrogation) by His saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith – We will join with them their descendants﴾. This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. This too is weak. The ruling of the verse is not lifted merely by the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas or anyone else that it is abrogated. The reconciling of the two verses is neither impossible nor unattainable, for the children follow the parents in the Hereafter just as they were followers of them in this world. This following is among the honor of the parents and the reward they attained by their striving. As for the children joining them in rank without striving on their part, this is not theirs; it is for the parents. Allah gladdened their eyes by joining their descendants with them in Paradise, and He graced the children with something that was not theirs, just as He graced the youths (wildan), the houris, and the creatures He creates for Paradise without deeds, and the people He admits to Paradise without any good they sent forward or any deed they performed.

So His saying: ﴿No bearer of burden will bear the burden of another﴾, and His saying: ﴿and that there is not for the human being except what he strove for﴾, are two decisive verses (muhkam) required by the justice of the Lord, His wisdom and His holy perfection, and reason and natural disposition (fitra) bear witness to both. The first requires that a person is not punished for another's crime. The second requires that a person does not succeed except by his own deed and striving. The first secures the servant from being seized for another's offense, as the kings of this world do. The second cuts off his hope of salvation through the deeds of his forefathers, predecessors and shaykhs, as is the case with the people of false hope. So reflect on the excellence of the combination of these two verses.

Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Whoever is guided, is only guided for his own self, and whoever goes astray, only goes astray to its detriment. No bearer of burden will bear the burden of another. And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾.

So He, glorified, decreed for His enemies four rulings which are the utmost of justice and wisdom:
The first: the guidance of the servants by faith and righteous deeds is for their own selves, not for others.
The second: their going astray, through the failure of that and falling short of it, is upon themselves, not upon others.
The third: no one is taken to account for another's offense.
The fourth: He does not punish anyone except after establishing the proof against him through His messengers.

So reflect on what is contained within these four rulings of His wisdom, justice and bounty, and in the refutation of the people of delusion and false hopes, and of those ignorant of Allah, His names and His attributes.

Another group said: what is meant by al-insan here is the living, not the dead. This too is of the first type in corruption.

All of this is from poor handling of a general term. One who handles it this way does not save his handling of the indications of words, carrying them against their original sense and what is understood from them. This handling is definitively corrupt, nullified by the context, by consideration (iʿtibar), by the principles and proofs of the Sharia, and by its custom. The cause of this bad handling is that its holder believes a view and then rejects whatever indicates the opposite by whatever means occur to him. So the evidences contrary to what he believes are treated as an attacker that he repels by any means, without caring by what. But the evidences of truth do not conflict or contradict one another; rather, some of them confirm others.

Another group said, and this is the answer of Abu al-Wafa ibn ʿAqil. He said: "The good answer in my view is to say: the human being, by his striving and good conduct, acquired friends, begot children, married wives, did good, and was kind to people, so they showed mercy to him and sent gifts of worship to him. This was the effect of his striving, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «Indeed the best of what a man eats is from his earnings, and indeed his child is from his earnings»."

And it is supported by his saying in the other hadith: «When a servant dies, his deeds are cut off except from three: knowledge from which benefit is derived after him, ongoing charity (sadaqa jariya) on his behalf, or a righteous child who supplicates for him».
