Another group said: what is meant by al-insan here is the living, not the dead. This too is of the first type in corruption.

All of this is from poor handling of a general term. One who handles it this way does not save his handling of the indications of words, carrying them against their original sense and what is understood from them. This handling is definitively corrupt, nullified by the context, by consideration (iʿtibar), by the principles and proofs of the Sharia, and by its custom. The cause of this bad handling is that its holder believes a view and then rejects whatever indicates the opposite by whatever means occur to him. So the evidences contrary to what he believes are treated as an attacker that he repels by any means, without caring by what. But the evidences of truth do not conflict or contradict one another; rather, some of them confirm others.

Another group said, and this is the answer of Abu al-Wafa ibn ʿAqil. He said: "The good answer in my view is to say: the human being, by his striving and good conduct, acquired friends, begot children, married wives, did good, and was kind to people, so they showed mercy to him and sent gifts of worship to him. This was the effect of his striving, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «Indeed the best of what a man eats is from his earnings, and indeed his child is from his earnings»."

And it is supported by his saying in the other hadith: «When a servant dies, his deeds are cut off except from three: knowledge from which benefit is derived after him, ongoing charity (sadaqa jariya) on his behalf, or a righteous child who supplicates for him».

From here comes the statement of al-Shafiʿi: if his child offers him the obedience of performing Hajj, that makes Hajj obligatory upon him, as if he had the provisions and mount in his wealth, unlike when a stranger offers it.

This is a middling answer that needs completion. The servant, by his faith and obedience to Allah and His Messenger, has striven to benefit from the deeds of his believing brothers, through his own deed, just as he benefits from their deeds in life alongside his own deed. The believers benefit from one another's deeds in the actions they share, such as prayer in congregation, for each of them has his prayer multiplied to twenty-seven times by the participation of another in the prayer. So the deed of another became a cause for an increase in his reward, just as his deed is a cause for an increase in the reward of another. Indeed, it has been said that the reward of prayer is multiplied by the return of worshippers. Likewise their joint participation in jihad, Hajj, enjoining good and forbidding evil, and cooperating in righteousness and piety. The Prophet ﷺ said: «The believer to the believer is like a building whose parts strengthen one another», and he interlaced his fingers.

It is known that this applies more to religious matters than to worldly ones. The Muslim's entry, together with the body of Muslims, into the covenant of Islam is among the greatest causes of the benefit of each Muslim reaching his companion, in his life and after his death. The supplication of the Muslims surrounds them from behind. Allah, glorified, informed of the bearers of the Throne and those around it that they seek forgiveness for the believers and supplicate for them. He informed of the supplication and seeking of forgiveness by His messengers for the believers, such as Noah, Abraham and Muhammad ﷺ.

So the servant, by his faith, has caused this supplication to reach him, so it is as if it were from his striving. What clarifies this is that Allah, glorified, made faith a cause for its holder to benefit from the supplication of his believing brothers and their striving. So when he brings it, he has striven in the cause that leads to it. The Prophet's saying to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs has indicated this: «If your father had affirmed monotheism, that would have benefited him», meaning the manumission (ʿitq) performed on his behalf after his death. So if he had brought the cause, he would have striven in a deed that leads to the reward of manumission. This is a subtle and very good approach.

Another group said: the Qur'an did not negate a man's benefit from the striving of another; it negated his ownership of other than his own striving. Between the two matters is a difference that is not hidden. He, Exalted, informed that a person owns only his striving. As for the striving of another, it belongs to its doer, who may give it to another if he wishes, or keep it for himself. He, glorified, did not say: "He benefits only from what he strove for." Our shaykh used to prefer and favor this approach.

[Section: Negation of the servant being punished for another's deed]

Likewise His saying: ﴿It has what it earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾, and His saying: ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾.

Moreover, this verse is more explicit in indicating that its context only negates the servant being punished for the deed of another and being seized for another's offense. For Allah, glorified, said: ﴿Today no soul will be wronged at all, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾. He negated being wronged, whether by having evil added to one's sins, or good subtracted from one's good deeds, or by being punished for another's deed. He did not negate benefiting from the deed of another, nor did He negate it in the manner of recompense. For the benefit one receives from what is given to him is not a recompense for his deed; rather, it is a charity that Allah bestows upon him and a favor from Him without striving on his part. Indeed He granted him that through the hand of some of His servants, not as a recompense.

[Section: Refutation of the argument from the cessation of deeds]

As for your argument with his saying ﷺ: «When the servant dies, his deed is cut off», it is a fallen argument. For he ﷺ did not say, "his benefit is cut off"; he informed only of the cessation of his deed. As for the deed of another, it belongs to its doer. If he gives it to him, the reward of the doer's deed reaches him, not the reward of his own deed. So what is cut off is one thing, and what reaches him is another. Likewise the other hadith: «Indeed, among what reaches the deceased from his good deeds and his works is...». So it does not negate that other things besides that reach him from the deeds and good deeds of others.

[Section: Refutation that gifting is a transfer (hawala, transfer of debt)]

As for your statement that gifting is a transfer (hawala), and a transfer is only with a binding right, this is the transfer of a creature onto a creature. As for the transfer of a creature onto the Creator, that is another matter, and it is not valid to analogize it to the transfer of servants onto one another. Is this not among the most invalid and corrupt analogies? What nullifies it is the consensus of the community on his benefit from fulfilling his debt and what is due upon him of rights, the discharge of the creditor's claim against him, charity and Hajj on his behalf, and a text that cannot be rejected or repelled. Likewise fasting. These corrupt analogies do not oppose the texts and principles of the Sharia.

[Section: Refutation of the one who said that preferring others with the reward is disliked]

As for your statement that preferring others with acts of worship is disliked, and this is the issue of preferring others with acts of nearness (qurab), then how about preferring others with the reward itself, which is the goal? It has been answered with several answers:

The first: the state of life is one in which the soundness of the outcome cannot be trusted, for it is possible that the living person may apostatize. Thus he would have given away an act of nearness to one who is not worthy of it. This is one who has been made secure by death.

If it is said: the one to whom the gift is made may also not have died in inward Islam, so he would not benefit from what is gifted to him. This is a question of utter falsehood, for gifting to him is of the same kind as praying over him, seeking forgiveness for him, and supplicating for him. If he is worthy, it benefits him; otherwise, the one who supplicates benefits alone.

The second answer: preferring others with acts of nearness indicates little desire for them and lagging behind in performing them. So if preferring others with them were permitted, it would lead to laziness, idleness and lagging behind. This is unlike the gifting of their reward, for the doer strives to earn it so that he may benefit from it or benefit his Muslim brother. Between them there is a clear difference.

The third: Allah, glorified, loves hastening and racing to serve Him and competing in it, for that is more eloquent in servanthood. Kings love eagerness and competition in obedience to them and in serving them. So preferring others with that contradicts the purpose of servanthood. For Allah, glorified, commanded His servant with this act of nearness, either as an obligation or as a recommendation. If he prefers others with it, he abandons what He commanded him and entrusts it to another. This is unlike when he does what he was commanded as obedience and nearness, and then sends its reward to his Muslim brother. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Race to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose width is like the width of the heaven and the earth﴾, and He said: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾. It is known that preferring others with them negates racing toward them and hastening to them.

The Companions used to race one another in acts of nearness, and none of them preferred another with them. ʿUmar said: "By Allah, Abu Bakr never outraced me to any good except that he outstripped me to it," until he said, "By Allah, I will never race you to good again."

And Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And for this let the competitors compete﴾. It is said: "nafastu fi'l-shay' munafasatan wa nifasan," when one desires a thing with a view to contest it. From this comes their saying "shay' nafis," meaning it is worthy of being competed for and desired. "Hadha anfas ma li" means this is the most beloved of my possessions to me. "Anfasani fulan fi kadha" means so-and-so made me desirous of it. All of this is the opposite of preferring others with it and turning away from it.

[Section: Refutation of the claim that if gifting to the dead is permissible, it would be permissible to the living]

As for your statement that if gifting to the dead were permissible, it would be permissible to the living, its answer has two aspects:

The first: some jurists among the companions of Ahmad and others went to that. The judge (al-Qadi) said: Ahmad's words do not imply restriction to the dead, for he said: "He does good and makes half of it for his father and mother," and did not distinguish. Abu al-Wafa ibn ʿAqil objected to this and said: "This is far-fetched. It is trifling with the Sharia, meddling with the trust of Allah, and a presumptuous claim against Allah, glorified, that a reward for a deed one does is transferred to another. After death, Allah has made for us a path to conveying benefit, such as seeking forgiveness and prayer over the dead."

Then he raised an objection against himself: "If it is said: is not the payment of a debt and bearing the burden during life like its payment after death? Thus the guarantee in life and the guarantee after death are equal, for both remove the demand from him. So if the payment of debts reaches him after death and during life, then make the reward of gifting reach him during life and after death."

He answered it: "If this were valid, sins would have to be expiated for the living by the repentance of others on their behalf, and the sins of the Hereafter would be removed by the deeds and seeking of forgiveness of others."

I say: this does not follow. Rather, it is a reflection (ṭard) against you: the living benefit from the supplication of others for them, from their seeking forgiveness for them, from their charity on their behalf, and from their payment of their debts. This is true, and the Prophet ﷺ permitted performing the obligatory Hajj on behalf of the living who is incapacitated (maʿdub) and the disabled, both of whom are living.

Other companions answered that during life we cannot trust the soundness of the outcome, for fear that the one to whom the gift is made may apostatize and so not benefit from what is gifted to him. Ibn ʿAqil said: "This excuse is void by the gift of the living, for it is not safe from the possibility that he may apostatize and die, nullifying all his deeds, including the reward of what was gifted to the dead."

I say: this does not bind them. The sources of the texts and consensus nullify and refute it. For the Prophet ﷺ permitted Hajj and fasting on behalf of the dead, and the people agreed on the discharge of the deceased's debt if the living pays it, despite the presence of the possibility that was mentioned.

The answer is to say: what he gifts of acts of righteousness to the dead has become his property. So it is not nullified by the apostasy of its doer after it has left his ownership, just like the dispositions he made before apostasy, such as manumission and expiation. Indeed, if he performed Hajj on behalf of an incapacitated person and then apostatized afterward, the incapacitated person is not obligated to have someone else perform Hajj on his behalf, for it is not safe to trust that in the second and third instances either.

Moreover, the difference between the living and the dead is that the living is not in need as the dead is in need, since he can himself perform that deed or its like. So he should earn the reward himself by his own striving, unlike the dead.

Also, it leads to some of the living relying on others, and this is a great corruption. For owners of wealth, if they understand that and sense it, will hire someone to perform it on their behalf. Thus acts of worship become transactions, and that leads to abandoning obligatory acts of worship and supererogatory ones, and what is drawn near to Allah becomes drawn near to human beings, departing from sincerity. So neither of them gains the reward.

We and others forbid taking a wage for every act of devotion, and we hold that taking pay for it nullifies its reward, as with judgeship, giving legal opinions (fatwa), teaching knowledge, prayer, reciting the Qur'an, and other acts. Allah confers reward only upon the sincere one who made his deed purely for His sake. If he does it for a wage, neither the doer nor the one who hires him is rewarded. It does not befit the excellent qualities of the Sharia that purely devotional acts for Him should become transactions aimed at exchange, earning, and worldly gain. The payment of debts and guaranteeing them differs, for they are rights of human beings, in which one person may stand in for another. Therefore it is permissible during life and after death.

[Section: Whether it is permissible to give as a gift half or a quarter of the reward]

As for your statement, "If that were permissible, then it would be permissible to give half or a quarter of the reward to the deceased," the response is twofold:

The first: denying the implication. You have not cited any evidence for it beyond mere assertion.

The second: accepting it and affirming it. This was explicitly stated by Imam Ahmad in the narration of Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Kahhal. The reasoning is that the reward is his property, so he may give all of it, and he may give part of it. It is further clarified by the fact that if he gave it to four people, for example, each of them would receive a quarter. So if he gives a quarter and keeps the remainder for himself, it is permissible, just as it is permissible to give it to someone else.

(Section)

As for your statement, "If that were permissible, then it would be permissible to give it after he has done the deed for himself, and you have said that he must intend at the time of the act that it be given to the deceased, otherwise it will not reach him."

The answer: this matter is not stated explicitly by Ahmad, nor is this condition found in the words of the earlier scholars among his companions. It was mentioned by later scholars such as al-Qadi and his followers.

Ibn 'Aqil said: If someone performs an act of obedience, such as prayer, fasting, or recitation of the Qur'an, and gifts it by making its reward for a deceased Muslim, it will reach him and benefit him, on condition that the intention to gift precedes the act or accompanies it.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Hamdan said in his al-Ri'aya: Whoever voluntarily performs an act of devotion, whether charity, prayer, fasting, Hajj, 'Umrah, recitation, manumission, or other physical acts of worship that admit of proxy, or financial acts of worship, and makes all or part of its reward for a deceased Muslim, even the Prophet (ﷺ), and supplicates for him, or asks forgiveness for him, or settles on his behalf a legal right or an obligation that admits of proxy, it benefits him and its reward reaches him. It is said: if he intends it at the time of the act or before it, it reaches him; otherwise it does not.

The essence of the matter is that the time at which the condition for the reward to be obtained is fulfilled is when it falls to the one to whom it is gifted first. It is possible that the reward first accrues to the doer and then transfers from him to another. So whoever makes it a condition that the intention be made before the act or before its completion, for the reward to reach the other, says: if he does not intend it, the reward accrues to the doer, and so its transfer from him to another is not accepted. For the reward is established by the deed the way an effect follows its cause. This is why, if someone frees a slave on his own behalf, the right of patronage (wala') belongs to him; if he then wished to transfer that patronage to someone else after the manumission, it would not transfer. By contrast, if he frees the slave on behalf of another, the patronage belongs to the one on whose behalf he freed him. Likewise, if he pays a debt on his own behalf and then after payment wishes to make it on behalf of another, he may not do so. Similarly, if he performs Hajj, fasts, or prays for himself, and then afterward wishes to make that on behalf of another, he does not have the right to do so. This is supported by the fact that those who asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this did not ask him about gifting the reward of an act after it has been performed; rather, they asked him about what they should do on behalf of the dead. As Sa'd said: "Will it benefit her if I give charity on her behalf?" He did not say, "If I gift the reward of what I gave in charity on my own behalf." Likewise the other woman's words: "Shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?" and the other man's words: "Shall I perform Hajj on behalf of my father?" He answered them by permitting the act on behalf of the dead, not by gifting the reward of what they had done for themselves to their dead. It is not known that the Prophet (ﷺ) was ever asked about the latter, nor is it known that any of the Companions did it, saying: "O Allah, make the reward of my deed, or the reward of what I did for myself, for so-and-so."

This is the wisdom of the condition, and it is the more discerning view. Whoever does not make this condition says: the reward belongs to the doer; so when he volunteers it and gifts it to another, it is like what he gives to that other from his wealth.

[Section: Refutation of the permissibility of gifting the reward of obligatory acts]

As for your statement, "If gifting were permissible, then it would be permissible to gift the reward of obligatory acts incumbent upon the living," the response is that this objection is untenable for one who makes the condition, for gifting the act on behalf of the dead, that the intention be on behalf of the deceased. For an obligatory act cannot validly be performed on behalf of another, since it is obligatory upon the doer, who must intend by it drawing near to Allah.

As for one who does not make the condition of intending the act on behalf of another, is it permissible in his view to make the reward of an obligatory act of his duties accrue to the deceased? On this there are two positions. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Hamdan said: It is said that if he makes the reward of an obligatory prayer, fast, or other obligation accrue to him, it is permissible and valid for the doer.

I say: It has been transmitted from a group of scholars that they made the reward of their deeds of obligation accrue to Muslims generally and said: "We meet Allah in poverty and utter destitution, and the Sharia does not prevent this. The reward is the property of the doer; if Allah wills that he give it to another, no restriction is placed on him in that. And Allah knows best."

[Section: Refutation of the claim that obligations are a test and trial]

As for your statement that obligations are a test and trial, which does not admit of substitution, since the aim of them is the very person of the obligated doer who acts, and so on.

The answer to this is that it does not prevent the Lawgiver from permitting a Muslim to benefit his brother with something of his deeds. Rather, this is part of the perfection of the Lord's beneficence and mercy toward His servants, and of the completeness of this Sharia which He has prescribed for them, which is founded on justice, kindness, and mutual support. The Lord, exalted is He, has appointed His angels and the bearers of His Throne to invoke blessings upon His believing servants, to ask forgiveness for them, and to ask Him to protect them from evil deeds. He commanded the seal of His messengers to ask forgiveness for the believing men and women, and He will raise him on the Day of Resurrection to a praised station in order to intercede for the sinners among his followers and the people of his Sunnah. He, exalted is He, commanded him to pray for his companions during their lives and after their deaths, and he would stand at their graves and supplicate for them.

The Sharia has settled that the sin which rests on all for abandoning the communal obligations (fard al-kifaya) falls away when it is performed by one through whose performance the purpose is achieved, even if it is only one person. He, glory be to Him, removed the pledge and the heat upon the skins in the grave by the living guaranteeing the debt of the dead and paying it on his behalf, even though that obligation is a test with respect to the one obligated. He permitted the Prophet (ﷺ) to allow Hajj and fasting on behalf of the dead, even though the obligation is a test with respect to him. He removed from the follower the prostration of forgetfulness by the validity of the imam's prayer and its freedom from forgetfulness, and the recitation of al-Fatiha by the imam's bearing it: he bears on behalf of the follower his forgetfulness and his recitation, and his covering of the imam's recitation is a recitation for those behind him and a covering for them. Is kindness toward the obligated person by gifting him the reward anything other than imitation of the kindness of the Lord, exalted is He? "And Allah loves the good-doers."

The creation are the servants of Allah, and the most beloved of them to Him are those most beneficial to His dependents. If He, glory be to Him, loves whoever benefits His dependents with a cup of water, a draught of milk, or a morsel of bread, how much more so whoever benefits them in their weakness, their poverty, the cessation of their deeds, and their need for something to be sent to them, at the time they most need it? So the most beloved of creation to Allah is whoever benefits His dependents in this state.

For this reason, a report has come from some of the early Muslims that whoever says every day seventy times, "My Lord, forgive me, my parents, the Muslim men and women, and the believing men and women," obtains a reward equal to the number of every Muslim man and woman and believer. Do not find this far-fetched, for when he asks forgiveness for his brothers he has done good to them, and Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.

[Section: Refutation of the claim that if another's deed benefited him, then his repentance would benefit him]

As for your statement that if another's deed benefited him, then his repentance and his Islam on his behalf would benefit him.

This objection is presented in two forms:

1. A form of implication in which the link between two matters is asserted, then the absence of the consequent is shown, so the antecedent is negated. Its form is this: If another's deed on his behalf benefited him, then his Islam and repentance on his behalf would benefit him; but they do not benefit him; therefore another's deed does not benefit him.

2. The second form: it is said that he does not benefit from another's Islam and repentance on his behalf; therefore he does not benefit from another's prayer, fasting, and recitation on his behalf.

It is known that this implication and pairing is certainly false.

As for first: it is an analogy that contradicts what the texts have concurred upon and what the Muslim community has agreed upon.

As for second: it combines what God has distinguished. For God, glory be to Him, distinguished between a person's Islam on behalf of another and his charity, Hajj, and manumission on behalf of another. The analogy that equates them is of the same kind as the analogy of those who equated carrion with slaughtered meat and usury with sale.

As for third: God, glory be to Him, made Islam a cause for Muslims benefiting one another during life and after death. If one does not bring the cause of benefiting from the deeds of Muslims, that benefit does not accrue to him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Amr: "If your father had acknowledged the Oneness of God and remained silent, or if you gave charity on his behalf, that would benefit him."

This is like God, glory be to Him, making Islam a cause for the servant benefiting from the good he has done. If he lacks this cause, the good of his deed does not benefit him and is not accepted from him. Just as He made sincerity and following the Sunnah a cause for the acceptance of deeds, so if they are lacking, deeds are not accepted; and just as He made the conditions of prayer a cause for its validity, so if they are lacking, validity is lost. This is the nature of all causes with their legal, rational, and sensory effects. Whoever equates two impossibilities, the existence of the cause and its absence, is in error.

An example of this absurdity is to say: If intercession were accepted for sinners, it would be accepted for polytheists; and if the people of major sins among the monotheists left the Fire, the disbelievers would leave it too. And similar analogies, which are among the filth of their proponents and the refuse of their mouths.

In sum: the scholars would do best to refrain from occupying themselves with repelling these ravings, were it not that they have blackened with them the pages of deeds and the pages that are among people.

[Section: Refutation of the claim that acts of worship are of two kinds]

As for your statement, "Acts of worship are of two kinds: one kind admits of proxy, so the reward of gifting it reaches the deceased; and another kind does not admit of it, so its reward does not reach him."

This is the very doctrine and claim itself, so how can you argue with it? From where do you have this distinction? What book, what Sunnah, or what consideration indicates it, such that it becomes obligatory to adopt it?

The Prophet (ﷺ) prescribed fasting on behalf of the dead, even though fasting does not admit of proxy. And he prescribed for the community that some of them stand in for others in performing a communal obligation: when one of them does it, the rest are relieved of it and the sin falls from them. And he prescribed for the guardian of a child who cannot understand that he may stand in for him in ihram and the rites of pilgrimage, and ruled that the child's status is through the act of his proxy.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The companions of one who has fainted become muhrim on his behalf; they treated the ihram of his companion as equivalent to his own. The Lawgiver made the Islam of the parents equivalent to the Islam of their children; likewise the Islam of the captor and the owner, according to the explicit position. You have seen how this complete Sharia extends the acts of righteousness from their doer to others. How, then, would it befit it to restrict a servant from benefiting his parents and showing mercy to his Muslim brothers, at the greatest times of their need, with some good and righteousness that he performs and whose reward he makes for them? And how would a servant restrict a broad matter, or restrict over the reward of his deed someone whom the Lawgiver has not restricted, or dispose of it as he wishes among the Muslims?

What brought the reward of Hajj, charity, and manumission to the dead is the very same thing that brings the reward of fasting, prayer, recitation, and seclusion: namely, the Islam of the one to whom the gift is made, the giving of the donor, his goodness, and the Lawgiver's not restricting him in goodness, but rather urging him to goodness by every means. The visions of believers have agreed and been transmitted with the greatest mass-transmission regarding the dead informing them that what they gift them of recitation, prayer, charity, Hajj, and other things reaches them. If we mentioned what has been related to us from people of our own age, and what has reached us from those before them of such things, it would be very lengthy.

And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I see that your visions have agreed that they are in the last ten nights."

So the Prophet (ﷺ) took into account the agreement of the believers' visions, just as one takes into account the agreement of their reports about what they witnessed. They do not lie in their reports nor in their visions when they agree.

[Section: Whoever dies while owing fasting]

As for the rejection of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) hadith, "Whoever dies while owing fasting, his guardian shall fast on his behalf," by those aspects which you have mentioned: we defend the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and show its agreement with the sound in those aspects. As for falsehood, its refutation suffices for us by its opposition to the sound, clear hadith whose spine cannot be bent, and there is no way to oppose it except by hearing, obeying, submitting, and accepting. We have no choice after it; rather, choice and all choice lies in submitting to it and affirming it, even if all from east to west opposed it.

As for your statement, "We reject it by the saying of Malik in his Muwatta: No one fasts on behalf of anyone." Your opponents say: rather, we reject this saying of Malik by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ). So which of the two parties is more deserving of correctness and better in refutation?

As for his statement, "And it is a matter agreed upon among us with no disagreement": Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, did not relate a consensus of the community from the East to the West of the earth. He only judged the view of the people of Madina by what reached him, and no disagreement among them had reached him. His lack of knowledge of disagreement on this point, may Allah have mercy on him, does not make void the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Indeed, even if all the people of Madina agreed on it, taking the hadith of the Infallible would be better than taking the view of the people of Madina, whose saying is not guaranteed infallibility for us beyond the community. Allah and His Messenger did not make their sayings a proof that must be referred to in a dispute. Rather, Allah, exalted is He, said: "And if you dispute about anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and more excellent in outcome" (Qur'an 4:59).

And even if Malik and the people of Madina said: "No one fasts on behalf of anyone," it has been related by al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba and Salama ibn Kuhayl from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas that he gave a legal ruling that for the making up of Ramadan one feeds on his behalf, and for a vow one fasts on his behalf.

This is the position of Imam Ahmad and many people of hadith, and it is the view of Abu 'Ubayd. Abu Thawr said: a vow and other than it is fasted on his behalf. Al-Hasan ibn Salih said regarding a vow: he fasts.

[Section: The statement of Ibn 'Abbas regarding the hadith on fasting]

As for your statement that Ibn 'Abbas is the narrator of the hadith on fasting on behalf of the dead, and he himself said: "No one fasts on behalf of anyone," the most this implies is that a Companion issued a legal ruling contrary to what he narrated. This does not discredit his narration, for his narration is protected from error, while his legal ruling is not protected. It is possible that he forgot the hadith, or interpreted it, or believed there was a stronger opposing evidence in his judgment, or other such reasons.

Moreover, Ibn 'Abbas's ruling does not in fact oppose the hadith, for he ruled in Ramadan that no one fasts on behalf of anyone, and he ruled regarding a vow that it is fasted on his behalf. This does not contradict his narration; rather, it confines the hadith to vows.

Furthermore, the hadith "Whoever dies while owing fasting, his guardian shall fast on his behalf" is established through the narration of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her. Suppose Ibn 'Abbas disagreed with it; so what? The disagreement of Ibn 'Abbas does not discredit the narration of the Mother of the Believers. Rather, rejecting Ibn 'Abbas's saying by the narration of 'A'isha is more appropriate than rejecting her narration by his saying.

Also, Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, has conflicting reports on this matter, with two narrations from him. So dropping the hadith in favor of the contrary report from him is no more appropriate than dropping that report in favor of the other narration from him.

[Section: The claim that the hadith is disputed in its chain]

As for your statement that it is a hadith whose chain is disputed, this is a reckless claim whose statement is not accepted. The hadith is sound, established, and agreed upon as sound; both of the two Sahihs narrated it, and its chain is not disputed.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever dies while owing fasting, his guardian shall fast on his behalf." Imam Ahmad declared it sound, adopted it, and al-Shafi'i conditioned the saying on its soundness. Something has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning fasting on behalf of the dead; if it is established, one fasts on his behalf just as one performs Hajj on his behalf. It has been established beyond doubt. This is the position of al-Shafi'i, as more than one of the leading scholars of his school have said. Al-Bayhaqi, after relating this wording from al-Shafi'i, said: The permissibility of making up for the dead has been established through the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and 'Ata', and from 'Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas. In the narration of most of them, a woman asked, and it seems to be a different story from the case of Umm Sa'd. In the narration of some of them: "Fast on behalf of your mother." This will be explained when answering his statement, may Allah have mercy on him.

As for your claim that it is contradicted by the explicit text of the Qur'an, namely His saying: "And that man has nothing except what he strove for" (Qur'an 53:39)...

I have translated the passage as it stands. Its main subjects are: a charge of bad manners and error against those who say the Sunnah contradicts the Qur'an; the hadith on fasting and feeding on behalf of the dead, and the weakness of the narration attributed to Ibn 'Umar; the views of scholars on fasting for the deceased; the reward of Hajj and of spending for it; whether the reward of gifts to the dead requires verbal intention; the superiority of various acts of gift; the reward of Qur'an recitation sent to the dead; and the question of gifts to the Prophet (ﷺ).

**Ibn al-Qayyim, Tafsir (Commentary on Surah an-Najm, 53:39–41), part 4 of 4**

It is a lapse of manners in expression and a grave error in meaning. Allah protects His Messenger (ﷺ) from having his Sunnah opposed by the texts of the Qur'an; rather, the Sunnah supports and confirms them. By Allah, what does partisanship and devotion to taqlid (blind imitation) accomplish?

What has preceded in the discussion of the verse is sufficient, and we have shown that there is no contradiction between it and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in any way. The apparent contradiction arises only from those who lack understanding. This is a grave and blameworthy method: rejecting established Sunnah on the basis of what is understood from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. The whole of knowledge lies in interpreting the Qur'an through the Sunnah, for the Sunnah is an explanation of it, derived from the one who brought it. It is not in contradiction with it.

As for your claim that it is opposed by what al-Nasa'i narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No one prays on behalf of another, and no one fasts on behalf of another, but for each day one mudd of wheat is to be fed on his behalf."

This is an ugly error. Al-Nasa'i narrated it thus: (Akhbarana) Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la, Hadathana Yazid ibn Zuray', Hadathana Hajjaj al-Ahwal, Hadathana Ayyub ibn Musa, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "No one prays on behalf of another, and no one fasts on behalf of another, but for each day one mudd of wheat is to be fed in his place." Thus it was narrated as the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, not the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is put forward against the established Sunnah despite the difference of narrations from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) never said these words; how could he say them?

It is established in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) that he said: "Whoever dies owing fasting, his guardian shall fast on his behalf." How could he say the first while in the hadith of Buraydah, which Muslim narrated in his Sahih, a woman said to him: "My mother died and owed a month of fasting?" He said: "Fast on behalf of your mother."

As for your claim that it is opposed by the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both): "Whoever dies owing the fasting of Ramadan, let food be given on his behalf." This is of the same kind; it is a false hadith attributed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Al-Bayhaqi said: The hadith of Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever dies owing the fasting of Ramadan, let food be given on his behalf," is not sound. Muhammad ibn al-Rahman frequently made errors. It was narrated by the companions of Nafi' from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) as his own statement.

As for your claim that it is opposed by the clear analogy with prayer, Islam and repentance, since no one performs these on behalf of another: by Allah, this analogy is manifestly invalid and corrupt, for it rejects the sound and explicit Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which testifies to its invalidity. We have explained the difference between accepting Islam on behalf of an unbeliever after his death and a Muslim benefiting from what his Muslim brother gifts him of the reward of fasting, charity or prayer. By Allah, the difference between them is too clear to be concealed. Is there any analogy more corrupt than equating a Muslim's benefit after death from what his brother gifts him of the reward of his deed with the acceptance of Islam for an unbeliever after his death, or the acceptance of repentance from a criminal after his death?

[Section: The permissibility of making up (qada') on behalf of the deceased]

As for the words of al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) in declaring the narrator of the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) mistaken, that the vow of Umm Sa'd was a fast, his foremost supporter al-Bayhaqi has answered him, and we will quote his words as they are.

He said in (Kitab al-Ma'rifa), after relating his words:

It is established that making up (qada') on behalf of the deceased is permissible, through the narrations of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). In the narration of most of them, a woman asked, and it is likely to be a different incident from the story of Umm Sa'd. In the narration of some of them: "Fast on behalf of your mother."

He said: Its soundness is confirmed by the narration of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ata' al-Madani, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Buraydah al-Aslami narrated to me from his father, who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) when a woman came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I had given a slave-girl in charity on behalf of my mother, and she died and the slave-girl remained.' He said: 'Your reward has been confirmed, and it has returned to you as an inheritance.' She said: 'She died and owed a month of fasting?' He said: 'Fast on behalf of your mother.' She said: 'She died and had not performed Hajj?' He said: 'Perform Hajj on behalf of your mother.'"

Muslim narrated it in his Sahih by several routes from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ata'. End of quotation.

I say: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us from al-A'mash, from Muslim al-Batin, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother died and owed a month of fasting; shall I make it up on her behalf?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If she had owed a debt, would you have paid it on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." He said: "The debt of Allah is more deserving of being paid."

Abu Khaythamah narrated it: Mu'awiyah ibn 'Amr narrated to us from Za'idah from al-A'mash, and he mentioned it. And al-Nasa'i narrated it from Qutaybah ibn Sa'd, from 'Abthar, from al-A'mash, and he mentioned it.

This is different from the hadith of Umm Sa'd in both chain and text. The story of Umm Sa'd was narrated by Malik from al-Zuhri from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd ibn 'Utbah from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): that Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "My mother died and had a vow upon her?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fulfil it on her behalf." Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated it thus in the two Sahihs.

Suppose that this is the preserved form of that hadith, that it was an unrestricted vow not specified. Would it then be the case in the hadith of al-A'mash from Muslim al-Batin from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not question Sa'd about the vow: whether it was prayer, charity or fasting, even though a vower may vow any of these? This indicates that there is no difference between making up a vow of fasting and one of prayer. Otherwise he would have asked him what the vow was, for if vows divide into two kinds, one that can be fulfilled on behalf of the deceased and one that cannot, there would be no room for not asking.

[Section: The views of scholars on fasting on behalf of the deceased]

We mention the views of the scholars on fasting on behalf of the deceased, lest one suppose that there is a consensus against it.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Fasting is performed on his behalf for a vow, and feeding is given on his behalf for missed Ramadan. This is the position of Imam Ahmad.

Abu Thawr said: Fasting is performed on his behalf for a vow and for an obligation. Likewise Dawud ibn 'Ali and his companions said: Fasting is performed on his behalf, whether it was a vow or an obligation.

The view of al-Awza'i: his guardian gives charity in place of the fast; if he cannot find the means, fasting is performed on his behalf. This is also the view of Sufyan in one of the two reports from him.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: Fasting is performed on his behalf for a vow, and feeding is given on his behalf for an obligation.

al-Hasan said: If he owed a month of fasting and thirty men fasted one day each on his behalf, it is permissible.

[Section: Refutation of the view that only the expense of Hajj reaches him as reward]

As for your claim that the reward of the expense of Hajj reaches him, but not the acts of the rites, this is a bare assertion without proof, and the Sunnah refutes it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Perform Hajj on behalf of your father," and he said to the woman: "Perform Hajj on behalf of your mother." Thus he informed that the Hajj itself is on the deceased's behalf, and he did not say that it is the expenditure that is credited to him.

Likewise he said to the one whom he heard reciting the talbiyah on behalf of Shubrumah: "Perform Hajj for yourself first, then perform Hajj on behalf of Shubrumah."

When the woman asked him about the child she had with her, she said: "Does this one perform Hajj?" He said: "Yes." He did not say that only the reward of expenditure is his; rather he informed that the child has a Hajj, though he had done nothing, and his guardian acts in his place in the acts of the rites.

Furthermore, the one who performs Hajj on behalf of the deceased may spend nothing on his journey beyond ordinary expenses; so what makes the expense of a stay or a journey count as the reward of the expense of Hajj for the one on whose behalf it is performed, when he did not spend it on Hajj? This view is refuted by the Sunnah and by analogy, and Allah knows best.

[Section: Pronouncing the intention of gifting a deed]

If it is asked: Do you require that the reward reach the deceased by a spoken formula of gifting, or is the intention of the doer to gift it to another sufficient for it to reach him?

It is answered: The Sunnah does not require a spoken formula of gifting in any single hadith. Rather, the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke of the act performed on behalf of another, such as fasting, Hajj and charity, without telling the doer to say: "O Allah, this is on behalf of so-and-so, son of so-and-so." Allah, glorified is He, knows the servant's intention and purpose by His knowledge. If he mentions it, that is permitted; if he omits mention and relies on the intention and purpose, it reaches him. He need not say: "O Allah, I am fasting tomorrow on behalf of so-and-so, son of so-and-so." This is why, Allah knows best, those who require intention for an act on behalf of another require it before the act, so that it is done for the deceased by intent.

As for one who does an act for himself and then intends to make its reward go to another, it does not pass to the other by intention alone, just as if one intended to give a gift, to free a slave, or to give charity, it would not be accomplished by intention alone.

What further clarifies this is that if one builds a place intending to make it a mosque, a school, a water-channel or the like, it becomes an endowment by the act together with intention, without need of a formula.

Likewise, if one gives money to a poor person with the intention of zakat, the zakat is discharged even if he does not pronounce it.

Likewise, if one pays a debt on behalf of another, living or dead, it is removed from the debtor's liability even if he does not say: "This is on behalf of so-and-so."

If it is asked: Is it obligatory to make the gift conditional, by saying: "O Allah, if You have accepted this deed and kept me steadfast in it, then make its reward for so-and-so," or not?

It is answered: That is not required, either in wording or in intention. Indeed, there is no benefit in the condition, for Allah does this whether or not one stipulates it. If He, glorified is He, did otherwise without the condition, the condition would have some benefit.

As for his saying: "O Allah, if You have kept me steadfast in this, then make its reward for so-and-so," this is based on the idea that the reward first falls to the doer and then passes from him to the one to whom it is gifted. That is not so. Rather, when the act is clearly for so-and-so, the reward first falls to the one for whom the act is done, just as if one frees one's slave on behalf of another: one does not say that the wala' (patronage) falls to the one who freed him and then passes from him to the one on whose behalf he was freed. It is the same here.

And success is from Allah.

If it is asked: Which is better, what one gifts to the dead? It is answered: The better is what benefits the deceased most. Freeing a slave and charity on his behalf are better than fasting on his behalf. The best charity is that which meets a real need of the recipient and is ongoing. This is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best charity is giving water to drink." This applies where water is scarce and thirst is common; otherwise, providing water by rivers is not better than feeding food when there is need. Likewise, supplication and seeking forgiveness for him, when it comes from a sincere, humble and devout supplicant, is in its place better than charity on his behalf, like the funeral prayer and standing to supplicate at his grave.

In sum, the best things to gift to the dead are freeing slaves, charity, seeking forgiveness for him, supplicating for him, and performing Hajj on his behalf.

As for reciting the Qur'an and gifting its reward to him voluntarily without payment, this reaches him just as the reward of fasting and Hajj reaches him.

If it is asked: This was not known among the early generations, and it cannot be transmitted from any one of them, despite their eagerness for good. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not direct them to it. He directed them to supplication, seeking forgiveness, charity, Hajj and fasting. Had the reward of recitation reached the dead, he would have directed them to it, and they would have done it.

The answer: The reply to this question depends on whether the questioner acknowledges that the reward of Hajj, fasting, supplication and seeking forgiveness reaches the dead. If so, it is said to him: What is this special quality that prevented the reward of recitation from reaching the dead, yet permitted the reward of the Qur'an and of these other acts to reach him? Is this anything but a distinction between things alike? If he does not acknowledge that those things reach the dead, he is refuted by the Book, the Sunnah, consensus and the principles of the Sharia.

As for the reason it did not appear among the early generations: they had no endowments for those who would recite and gift to the dead, and they did not know of it at all. They used to go to the grave to recite there, as people do today, and none of them would testify before those present that the reward of this recitation, or of this charity or fast, was for so-and-so, the deceased.

Then it is said to this speaker: If you were asked to quote from one of the early generations that he said: "O Allah, the reward of this fast is for so-and-so," you would be unable to do so. The people were the most averse of all to making known their good deeds, so they would not testify before Allah that its reward reached their dead.

If it is asked: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) directed them to fasting, charity and Hajj, but not to recitation.

The answer: He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not begin with this; rather, it came from him as a reply to them. One asked him about Hajj on behalf of a dead woman, and he permitted it; another asked about fasting on her behalf, and he permitted it; another asked about charity, and he permitted it. He did not prohibit them from anything beyond that.

And what difference is there between the reward of fasting, which is mere intention and abstention, and the reward of recitation and remembrance?

As for the claim that no one among the early generations did that, it is the claim of one who speaks without knowledge, for it is testimony to the negation of what one does not know. How does he know that the early generations did not do it without those present testifying to it? The knowledge of the Knower of the unseen of their intentions and purposes suffices, especially since, as previously stated, pronouncing the intention of gifting is not required.

The secret of the matter is that the reward belongs to the doer. When he gives it freely and gifts it to his Muslim brother, Allah conveys it to him. What then singles out the reward of reciting the Qur'an, and forbids the servant from conveying it to his brother? This is the practice of all people throughout all ages and lands, including the reprehensible, without any objection from the scholars.

If it is asked: What do you say about gifting to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?

It is answered: Among the later jurists, some recommended it and others did not, considering it an innovation, since the Companions did not do it. The Prophet (ﷺ) has a reward like that of everyone in his community who performs a good deed, without diminishing the reward of the doer at all, for he is the one who guided his community to every good, directed them to it and called them to it. Whoever calls to guidance has a reward like that of those who follow him, without any diminution of their rewards. Every guidance and knowledge that his community attained, they attained through him; so he has a reward like that of whoever follows him, whether or not he is gifted it.

And Allah knows best.

**Section**

Ahmad [ibn Hanbal] was asked about a man who does a good deed and gives half of its reward to his father or to his mother. He said: "I hope [it reaches them]."

He also said: "Everything good reaches the dead, because of what has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'Among the acts of righteousness after the righteous acts is that you pray for them along with your prayer, fast for them along with your fast, and give charity on their behalf along with your charity.'" End of quotation.

It is not required to name the person to whom the reward is gifted; intention suffices. He stated this in the narration of his son Abdullah: "There is no harm in performing Hajj on behalf of a man without naming him."

**[Section: The arrival of the reward of charity]**

As for the arrival of the reward of charity, (it is in the two Sahihs [Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim]) from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother died suddenly without making a bequest, and I think that if she had been able to speak, she would have given charity. Will she have a reward if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." (1)

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Sa'd ibn Ubadah's mother died while he was absent from her. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother has died while I was absent from her. Will it benefit her if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then I call you to witness that my garden, al-Mikhraf, is a charity on her behalf." (2)

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah: a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "My father died and left wealth, and he did not make a bequest. Will it expiate for him if I give charity on his behalf?" He said: "Yes."

In the Sunan and in Musnad Ahmad, from Sa'd ibn Ubadah, that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, Sa'd's mother has died; which charity is best?" He said: "Water." So he dug a well and said: "This is for the mother of Sa'd."

From Abdullah ibn Amr: al-As ibn Wa'il vowed in the pre-Islamic period to sacrifice one hundred camels, and Hisham ibn al-As sacrificed fifty-five. Amr asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about that, and he said: "As for your father, had he affirmed the Oneness [of Allah], then fasting on his behalf and giving charity on his behalf would have benefited him." Related by Imam Ahmad.

**[Section: The arrival of the reward of fasting]**

As for the arrival of the reward of fasting, (it is in the two Sahihs) from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies owing fasts, his guardian shall fast on his behalf." (1)

(And in the two Sahihs) also from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother died and owed a month of fasting. Shall I make it up on her behalf?" He said: "If your mother had a debt, would you have paid it?" He said: "Yes." (2) He said: "The debt owed to Allah is more deserving of being paid." (3)

In another narration: A woman came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother died and owed fasts for a vow. Shall I fast on her behalf?" He said: "Do you see, if your mother had a debt and you paid it, would that have discharged it for her?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then fast on behalf of your mother." This wording is that of al-Bukhari alone, as a suspended (mu'allaq) narration. (4)

From Bureydah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "While I was sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a woman came to him and said: 'I gave my mother a slave-girl as charity, and she has died.' He said: 'Your reward is due, and the inheritance has returned it to you.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, she owed a month of fasting; shall I fast on her behalf?' He said: 'Fast on her behalf.' She said: 'She never performed Hajj; shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?' He said: 'Perform Hajj on her behalf.'" Related by Muslim. In another wording: "two months of fasting." (5)

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a woman boarded a ship and vowed that if Allah saved her, she would fast for a month. Allah saved her, but she did not fast until she died. Then her daughter or her sister came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he commanded her to fast on her behalf. Related by the authors of the Sunan and by Imam Ahmad.

Likewise, it has been related from him (ﷺ) that the reward of a substitute for fasting, which is feeding the poor, reaches the dead.

In the Sunan, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies owing a month of fasting, let him feed a poor person on his behalf for each day." Related by al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah. Al-Tirmidhi said: "We do not know it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) narration except through this route, and the sound report from Ibn Umar is his own statement, mawquf (halted at the companion)." (1)

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "If a man falls ill during Ramadan and does not fast, food is given on his behalf and there is no makeup obligation. If he owed a vow, his guardian makes it up on his behalf." (2) (3)

**[Section: The arrival of the reward of Hajj]**

As for the arrival of the reward of Hajj, in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a woman from Juhaynah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My mother vowed to perform Hajj but died without performing it. Shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?" He said: "Perform Hajj on her behalf. Do you see, if your mother had a debt, would you have paid it? Pay what is owed to Allah, for Allah is more deserving of being paid." (4)

The narration of Bureydah has already been mentioned, in which [the woman said]: "My mother did not perform Hajj; shall I perform Hajj on her behalf?" He said: "Perform Hajj on her behalf."

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The woman of Sinan ibn Salamah al-Juhani was commanded to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that her mother had died without performing Hajj: "Is it sufficient that she perform Hajj on her behalf?" He said: "Yes. If your mother had a debt and you paid it on her behalf, would that not have sufficed for her? So let her perform Hajj on behalf of her mother." Related by al-Nasa'i. (5)

It has also been related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a woman asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about her father who died without performing Hajj. He said: "Perform Hajj on behalf of your father."

It has also been related from him, who said: A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, my father died without performing Hajj; shall I perform Hajj on his behalf?" He said: "Do you see, if your father had a debt, would you have paid it?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then the debt owed to Allah is more deserving."

The Muslims have agreed that the payment of a debt discharges it from the debtor's liability, even if it is paid by a stranger or from outside his estate. The narration of Abu Qatadah also indicates this, when he guaranteed two dinars on behalf of the deceased, and when he paid them the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Now his skin has cooled." (6)

They have also agreed that if a living person has a right against a deceased person, and the living person forgives it, that benefits the deceased and frees him from it, just as it discharges the liability of a living debtor.

So if it is discharged from the liability of a living debtor by textual evidence and consensus, even when it is possible for the creditor to collect it personally, and even if he does not consent but refuses it, then its discharge from the liability of a deceased person by pardon, when he cannot pay it, is more fitting and more deserving. And if the deceased benefits from pardon and remission, then likewise he benefits from a gift and an offering. There is no difference between them. For the reward of an act is the right of the one who offers it and gives it; so if he makes it for the deceased, it passes to him, just as the rights owed by the deceased, whether debt or otherwise, are purely the right of the living; so if he forgives them, the forgiveness reaches the deceased and he is released from liability. Both are rights of the living. So what text, analogy (qiyas), or rule of the Sharia requires the arrival of one of them while preventing the arrival of the other?

These texts are consistent in establishing that the rewards of deeds reach the dead when the living perform them on their behalf. This is pure analogy: the reward is the right of the one who performs the act, so if he gives it to his Muslim brother, he is not prevented from doing so, just as he is not prevented from giving away his property during his life or forgiving a debt after his death.

The Prophet (ﷺ) has indicated the arrival of the reward of fasting, which is merely abstention and an intention established in the heart that no one knows of but Allah, and which is not an act of the limbs. Then the arrival of the reward of recitation, which is an act of the tongue heard by the ear and seen by the eye, is all the more fitting. This is further clarified by the fact that fasting is pure intention and restraining oneself from the things that break the fast; and Allah has caused its reward to reach the dead. How much more so recitation, which is an act and an intention, and indeed does not require intention. So the arrival of the reward of fasting to the dead indicates the arrival of all other deeds.

Acts of worship are of two kinds: financial and physical. The Lawgiver has indicated, by the arrival of the reward of charity, the arrival of the reward of all other financial acts of worship, and by the arrival of the reward of fasting, the arrival of all other physical acts of worship; and he informed that the reward of Hajj, which combines the financial and the physical, arrives. So the three categories are established by textual evidence and reasoned inference. And success is from Allah.

**[The arguments of those who deny arrival]**

Those who deny the arrival [of rewards] said: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ (1). He also said: ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾ (2). And He said: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾ (3). It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When a servant dies, his deeds end, except for three: an ongoing charity, a righteous child who prays for him, or knowledge from which people benefit after him." (4) So he informed that a person benefits only from what he was the cause of during his life; and what he was not the cause of has ended for him.

Also, the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned earlier, which is his saying: "Among what reaches a dead person from his deeds and good works after his death is knowledge that he spread." This hadith indicates that he benefits only from what he himself caused.

Likewise the hadith of Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Seven things whose reward continues to flow to the servant while he is in his grave after his death: one who taught knowledge, or dug a canal, or dug a well, or planted a palm tree, or built a mosque, or left a copy of the Qur'an as an inheritance, or left a righteous child who asks forgiveness for him after his death." This indicates that anything beyond these does not yield him reward; otherwise the enumeration would have no meaning.

They said: Offering is a transfer (hawalah), and a transfer is only valid for a binding right, while deeds do not necessitate reward; it is merely Allah's grace and kindness. How then can a servant transfer to another what is merely grace, which is not obligatory upon Allah? Rather, if He wills He gives it, and if He does not will, He does not give it. This is like the transfer of a poor man to someone he hopes will give him charity. Such a thing is not valid to offer or to give as a gift, like a gift hoped for from a king which is not certain to be received.

They said: Also, preferring others with the means of reward is disliked, and that is preferring others with acts of devotion. How much more so preferring others with the reward itself, which is the goal? If preferring others with the means is disliked, then the goal is more fitting [to be disliked]. Likewise Imam Ahmad disliked delaying from the first row and giving it up to a grave, because of the desire to avoid the cause of reward.

Ahmad said in the narration of Hanbal, when he was asked about a man who delays from the first row and lets his father take his place there: "I do not like it. He can be dutiful to his father without this."

They said: Also, if it were permissible to offer [reward] to the dead, it would be permissible to transfer the reward and offer it to the living. Also, if that were permissible, then a half of the reward, or a quarter of it, or a qirat of it, would be permissible for him.

Also, if that were permissible, it would be permissible to offer it after performing the act for oneself. And you have said that one must intend, at the time of the act, to offer it to the dead, otherwise it does not reach him. So if it is permissible for him to transfer the reward, what difference is there between intending before the act or after it?

Also, if offering were permissible, it would be permissible to offer the reward of obligatory acts by the living, just as it is permissible to offer the reward of the voluntary acts one performs.

They said: Obligations are a test and a trial that do not accept substitution, for their purpose is the very person of the responsible one who acts, is commanded and forbidden. So the responsible one under test is not replaced by another, nor does another stand in for him in that, since the purpose is his own obedience and his own servitude. If he could benefit from another's offering without any act on his part, the Most Generous of the generous would be more worthy of that. And He, glorified be He, has decreed that a person benefits only from seven things, and this is His way with His creation and His decree, just as it is His way with His command and His law. A sick man is not represented by another in drinking medicine, and a hungry, thirsty, or naked person is not represented by another in eating, drinking, or clothing. They said: If the act of another benefited him, then his repentance would benefit him in that way.

They said: For this reason, Allah does not accept the Islam of one person on behalf of another, nor his ritual purity on behalf of another's. So if the very foundation of acts of worship cannot have its reward offered, how much less its branches?

[The one who holds this view] said: As for supplication, it is a request and an expression of desire to Allah that He bestow His grace upon the dead, pardon him, and forgive him; and this is the offering of the reward of the living's act to him.

**[The position of those who restrict arrival to acts in which substitution is admissible]**

Those who restrict the arrival [of reward] to acts of worship that admit substitution, such as charity and Hajj, said: Acts of worship are of two kinds:

One kind does not admit substitution at all, such as Islam, prayer, recitation of the Qur'an, and fasting. The reward of this kind belongs exclusively to its doer and is not transferred or passed on from him, just as during his life no one performs it on behalf of another, and no one stands in for its doer.

Another kind admits substitution, such as returning deposits, paying debts, giving out charity, and Hajj. The reward of this reaches the dead, because it admits substitution, and a servant performs it on behalf of another during his life; so after his death it is all the more so, and in every way.

They said: As for the hadith, "Whoever dies owing fasts, his guardian shall fast on his behalf," its answer is in several ways:

First: What Malik said in his Muwatta': "No one fasts on behalf of anyone else." He said: "This is a matter agreed upon among us, with no disagreement about it."

Second: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is the one who related the hadith about fasting on behalf of the dead, yet al-Nasa'i related from him: (We were informed by) Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la, who said: Yazid ibn Zurai' told us, who said: Hajjaj al-Ahwal told us, who said: Ayyub ibn Musa told us, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "No one prays on behalf of anyone else."

Third: It is a hadith whose chain is disputed, as the author of al-Mufhim in his commentary on Muslim said.

Fourth: It contradicts the text of the Qur'an, as mentioned above, in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾.

Fifth: It contradicts what al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No one prays on behalf of anyone else, and no one fasts on behalf of anyone else; but one feeds on his behalf a mudd of wheat for each day."

Sixth: It contradicts the hadith of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever dies owing the fasts of Ramadan, let food be given on his behalf."

Seventh: It contradicts clear analogy regarding prayer, Islam, and repentance, for no one performs them on behalf of another.

Al-Shafi'i said, in what he said about the report of Ibn Abbas, without naming Ibn Abbas: "What was the vow of the mother of Sa'd? It is possible that it was a vow of Hajj, or 'umrah, or charity, and he commanded him to fulfil it on her behalf. As for one who vows prayer or fasting and then dies, he makes expiation for it in the case of fasting, but fasting is not performed on his behalf, nor is prayer performed on his behalf, nor is expiation made for it in the case of prayer." Then he said: "If it is said: Has it been related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he commanded someone to fast on behalf of another?" It is answered: "Yes, Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, related it from the Prophet (ﷺ)." If it is said: "Then why do you not act upon it?" It is answered: The hadith of al-Zuhri from Ubayd Allah from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), [mentions] a vow and does not name it, despite al-Zuhri's memorization and Ubayd Allah's long companionship with Ibn Abbas. When another related it from a man, from Ibn Abbas, with wording different from the hadith of Ubayd Allah, it is more likely that it is not preserved." If it is said: "Then identify the man who brought this hadith, who erred regarding Ibn Abbas." It is answered: "Yes: the companions of Ibn Abbas related from Ibn Abbas that he said to Ibn al-Zubayr: 'Al-Zubayr released himself from the Hajj tamattu',' and this was related from Ibn Abbas as [referring to] the enjoyment of women; and this is a gross error."

This is the answer regarding the act of fasting. As for the act of Hajj, only the reward of the expenditure reaches the dead; and as for the acts of the rites, they are like the acts of prayer, which only their doer performs.

**[The reply of the proponents of arrival]**

The proponents of arrival said: Nothing in what you have mentioned contradicts the evidence of the Book and the Sunnah, the consensus of the early community, and the requirements of the rules of the Sharia. We answer everything you have mentioned with justice and fairness.

As for the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾:

People have differed regarding the meaning of the verse. One group said: the word "man" here means the disbeliever; as for the believer, he has what he strove for and what was strived for on his behalf, by the evidence we have mentioned. They said: The most that this restriction involves is that it is permissible, since evidence indicates it.

This answer is very weak. A general term like this is not meant to refer to the disbeliever alone; rather it includes both the Muslim and the disbeliever, and it is like the general term before it, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ (1).

The whole context, from beginning to end, is virtually explicit in intending the general sense, because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And that his striving will be seen, then he will be recompensed with the fullest recompense﴾ (2). This certainly encompasses both good and evil, and it includes the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ (3).

And like His saying in the divine hadith: "O My servants, these are only your deeds, which I count for you and then repay you in full. So whoever finds good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds other than that, let him blame no one but himself." And it is like His saying the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet it﴾ (4).
